The Crown Signia, bZ Woodland, Grand Highlander, RAV4, and Sienna get prepped for the great outdoors with mild but effective mods.

The whole “getting outside” thing has seen an enormous resurgence in popularity in recent years, so Toyota figured it couldn’t go wrong by modifying a handful of its mainstream models to reflect the crunchy vibe.

Naturally, the project was entrusted to the staff of its CALTY Design Research arm, who explored the idea of how daily drivers—primarily the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, bZ Woodland, and Crown Signia—could be modified to better perform in and near the boonies without compromising their on-road comfort and usability.

Despite their obvious differences, the team started with a single-shot approach covering each model in a coat of Horizon Blue paint, inspired by a hue used in the 1960s on Toyota models like the Stout, Crown, and Corona. #4504. The Ford Escape may return as an EV based on the UEV platform [Update]

Ford pulled the plug on the Escape last year after a 25-year run, but the crossover SUV could return as an EV on the new UEV platform.

While Ford is preparing to launch the Fathom, its first vehicle based on the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform in 2027, the company is already hinting at what could be its second UEV-based model.

The last gas-powered Escape models rolled off the production line at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant as it retooled the facility to prepare for the new Fathom electric pickup.

Typically, when Ford retires a model, its landing page says something like “we’re discontinuing” it, or “it’s the end of the road,” such as with the Edge SUV.

Meanwhile, the Escape landing page says the “SUV may be taking a breather for now,” declaring the “Ford Escape is tapping the brakes,” with no mention of it being discontinued. Instead, the site directs you to check out Ford’s other vehicles while it’s on hiatus.

According to Ford Authority, the Escape will return as an all-electric crossover SUV based on the UEV platform.

Update 10/29/2026: A Ford spokesperson told Electrek that the Ford Authority report is pure speculation and the company has not announced the Escape will return as an EV or that it will be based on the UEV platform.

If it does come to life, the Ford Escape EV would likely remain close in size to the outgoing gas model, which measures 180.1″ long, 74.1″ wide (without mirrors), and 66.1″ tall, with a 106.7″ wheelbase. That’s about the size of other compact SUVs like the Toyota RAV4 and Hyundai Tucson.

The report claimed the electric Escape is expected to enter production at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in 2029, possibly making it the second vehicle based on its UEV platform, following the Fathom pickup.

CEO Jim Farley confirmed on Ford’s Q3 earnings call on Wednesday that the Fathom launch “remains on track for the fourth quarter of next year.”

The Fathom is “a breakthrough product,” Farley said, adding the pickup is highly capable, innovative, and affordable.

Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range version. With the $1,595 delivery fee, Ford’s electric pickup will still start under $30,000, which the company says will be “right in the heart of the market.”

The Fathom will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps into its navigation system. It will also be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving. Other standard features include Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.

Ford claims the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, not including the added bed and frunk (front trunk).

2029 seems a little slow, but I'm glad Ford is still pushing ahead with EV plans.

Inside, the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with an easy-to-use navigation system using Apple Maps.

Ford has yet to reveal battery specs or range, but the UEV platform uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to reduce costs. We also know the Fathom will have an NACS charge port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

The UEV platform is flexible enough to underpin vehicles ranging from compact crossovers to pickup trucks and vans, so an electric Escape would make sense.

With the Fathom set to launch next year, we should learn more about the potential Ford Escape EV soon. Check back for updates.

Chevrolet is continuing its strategic push into the law enforcement sector with a first look at the 2027 Chevy Silverado Police Pursuit Vehicle (PPV). As police departments across the country increasingly phase out traditional sedans in favor of larger, more capable trucks, this pursuit-rated pickup is heavily positioned as a versatile fleet option. Building directly on the successful foundation established when the 2023 Chevy Silverado PPV was revealed, the 2027 iteration introduces updated front-end styling and heavy-duty interior features specifically engineered to accommodate bulky utility belts and complex radio setups.

The broad transition toward full-size trucks for daily patrol duty allows departments to utilize vehicles fully capable of clearing curbs, safely transporting hundreds of pounds of tactical gear, and withstanding severe daily wear and tear. Equipped with heavy-duty steel wheels, massive 16-inch Brembo brakes, and a standard locking rear differential, the 2027 Silverado PPV is expressly built for demanding municipal use.

While several competing automakers are actively introducing electric options to municipal fleets, Chevrolet is maintaining a strict focus on traditional internal combustion for highway patrol units that require sustained power and rapid refueling capabilities. Specs from a report from GM Authority show that the 2027 Silverado PPV is powered by a robust 5.3-liter V8 engine producing a reliable 355 horsepower. This proven powerplant is mated to a heavy-duty 10-speed automatic transmission and a high-capacity alternator necessary for continuously running emergency lighting and communication equipment over grueling shifts.

Fleet managers heavily prioritize proven, reliable platforms to minimize vehicle downtime. Following highly publicized reports that the some Police Squads are having bad luck with their Dodge Durangos due to unexpected mechanical issues, proven powertrain options remain a major selling point for Chevrolet’s commercial and heavy-duty truck division.

To meet strict law enforcement standards, the Silverado PPV utilizes a specially tuned suspension system that noticeably lowers the truck’s ride height for substantially improved high-speed stability. It is officially pursuit-rated by the manufacturer to reach top speeds of 112 mph, having undergone rigorous independent testing to ensure it can safely handle aggressive cornering and extreme braking without excessive brake fade.

This dedicated factory tuning is absolutely essential for officer safety and departmental liability management. In sharp contrast to standard civilian performance models occasionally pressed into service, like this California Camaro cop car that is banned from sport and track modes due to restrictive departmental policy, the Silverado PPV is explicitly engineered and fully warrantied to operate safely at its mechanical limits during active pursuits. By effectively balancing heavy-duty utility with pursuit-rated high-speed stability, the 2027 Silverado PPV provides modern departments with a highly capable, purpose-built patrol option.

#4501. This $15,000 low-speed EV is now on sale, and it’s street-legal

It may be small, but it’s already drawing a big response. The 2027 Fiat Topolino is now on sale in the US: a street-legal, low-speed EV that starts under $15,000.

With many dealers selling out of the first batch of 2026 models, the Fiat Topolino (which we already had a chance to test out) is back for 2027, bringing a new Open Air body style and color options.

The Topolino is even smaller than the Fiat 500e, measuring just over 8 feet (8’3″) long. That’s slightly longer than the average golf cart, but it can be driven legally on the street.

Federally classified as a motor vehicle, the Topolino is street-legal and can be driven on most public roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less. While you won’t be taking it on the highway, it’s perfect for driving around neighborhoods and beach towns, golf communities, campgrounds, and more.

Using a 5.4 kWh lithium-ion battery and an 8 hp electric motor, the Topolino can drive up to 46 miles on a single charge with a top speed of 25 mph. A full recharge using a standard outlet takes about five hours.

The 2027 Fiat Topolino is now available at select US dealers, starting at $14,985, including the destination fee.

You can choose from three different body styles: Topolino, Dolce Vita, and a new Open Air model. The new Open Air version has the Dolce Vita’s roll-back soft-top roof and asymmetrical full doors, like the standard Topolino.

Before everyone jumps on the "I can't drive it 500 miles away at 100mph" train, back in the day, my in-laws towed a Jeep behind their RV. This would be a perfect version of that.

Fiat is offering a free LSV conversion kit, which includes a rearview mirror, a backup camera, and a pedestrian alert system to make it street legal.

Unlike the initial batch of 2026 models, the 2027 Fiat Topolino will arrive at dealers as already street legal. Fiat is also offering complimentary home delivery for those who live within a 50-mile radius of the dealer.

You can learn more about the Topolino or pre-order yours on Fiat’s website.

Volkswagen went through very choppy waters in 2025, but 2026 has been anything but kind to Germany’s biggest automaker. In the third quarter of this year, it posted massive losses amounting to $6.6 billion. It posted profits of nearly $4 billion in the second quarter and $2.8 billion in the first quarter, but the most recent financial report reveals everything it had gained had practically been wiped out.

It’s been one problem after another for VW, as it needs to cut costs amidst plunging sales, the beating it’s getting in China, and resistance from workers’ unions due to mass layoffs. With the way things are going, projects are bound to be suspended, or worse, canceled altogether.

With all of that going on, one project that has been put on ice is the electric Golf. Reuters noted VW Passenger Cars CEO Thomas Schäfer during the earnings call, saying, “I know what the Golf means for Volkswagen and for Wolfsburg. That’s why this decision was really not an easy one for us.”

It’s a major blow to the automaker’s EV push, especially given that its subcompact EVs are actually making headway. The ID. Polo has already raked in a whole lot of orders, and the reviews so far are actually positive. That’s something that couldn’t be said about VW’s initial attempts at mass-market EVs. The electric Golf, likely to be called the ID. Golf, could have carried the momentum that the ID. Polo and ID. Cross have been gathering, but alas, it won’t be the case right away. That’s a bit of a shame given that it was being hyped up just a few months ago. Based on the previous report, it will follow the form of the MK. 4 Golf, and it will have a button-rich cabin like the subcompact EVs.

The ID. Golf does, indeed, sound promising, but we won’t know what it would be like for the next couple of years, and that’s if development for it pushes through. Right now, though, there are more urgent matters that VW has to attend to before moving forward.

#4499. Ex-Tesla Autopilot head calls vision-only a ‘weird religious stance’

GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, who ran Tesla’s Autopilot program in 2015 and 2016, says dropping radar for a camera-only self-driving system is “a weird religious stance that ignores physics.”

It’s the bluntest rebuke of Tesla’s vision-only bet yet from someone who helped build the original Autopilot. And it lands while Tesla is pushing camera-only Cybercabs into driverless service in Austin.

Anderson made the comments in an interview with The Verge published October 27, after GM’s technology event in New York the week before. Asked whether GM could eventually move to a vision-only approach like Tesla’s, he didn’t leave much room for interpretation.

“If you scale back to vision-only, physics suggests you’ll be in trouble in certain situations,” Anderson said. He added that radar is so cheap that removing it makes no sense, and that “cameras can’t see through dense fog or measure instantaneous velocity like radar can.”

He also said lidar helps camera systems improve faster when the two are trained together. That’s a direct counter to Tesla’s argument that cameras plus fleet data are all you need.

Anderson isn’t a lidar startup CEO talking his book. He led the Model X program at Tesla, then directed Autopilot during its formative years before co-founding self-driving company Aurora. GM hired him as chief product officer in 2025, and Bloomberg reported last year that Mary Barra sees him as a frontrunner to become GM’s next CEO.

His roadmap at GM goes the other way from Tesla’s. The Cadillac Escalade IQ is due to debut GM’s “eyes-off” system in 2028, with lidar, radar, and cameras.

He took a shot at another Tesla habit in the same interview. Anderson said he avoids “eyes off” marketing language altogether, arguing that a driver-assist system that feels very capable already pushes drivers into complacency. That’s the core problem with selling “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”

Tesla started pulling radar from Model 3 and Model Y in May 2021. Tesla Vision launched with limitations: Autosteer capped at 75 mph, a longer minimum following distance, and Smart Summon and Emergency Lane Departure Avoidance disabled at delivery. Ultrasonic sensors went next, in 2022.

The decision wasn’t unanimous inside Tesla. Former employees said engineers tried to convince Elon Musk not to drop radar, and he overruled them. Musk told Electrek at the time that “a very high resolution radar would be better than pure vision, but such a radar does not exist.” We argued that there are plenty of high resolution radars these days.

But the bigger problem is the exact one Anderson named: visibility.

In March, NHTSA upgraded its investigation into FSD in reduced-visibility conditions to an Engineering Analysis covering 3,203,754 vehicles, the last step before a recall. The probe now counts nine crashes, including a pedestrian killed in November 2023. NHTSA found FSD’s camera degradation detection “did not detect common roadway conditions that impaired camera visibility,” including sun glare, fog, and airborne dust, and only alerted drivers right before the crashes.

Radar doesn’t care about sun glare. That’s the point of redundancy.

As a human with 40+ years of driving with vision only, on dark rural roads in bad weather, there have been plenty of times when I had a few moments of confusion / optical illusion. The main thing I've learned is not to panic or make sudden inputs, maybe just let off the gas. The road probably does what it logically should do. Within a few seconds, the real situation usually becomes clear.

My point in saying this is that vision only isn't great, even for humans. I'm not sure a machine can be trained to handle these moments well, and requiring an unprepared "driver" to step in at the last second cannot be expected to end well.

Anderson is right, and he’s in a better position than almost anyone to say it. He ran Autopilot back when it still used radar.

The vision-only case always rested on a tidy idea: humans drive with two eyes, so cameras and enough AI should do the job. But humans crash in fog and glare too, and the promise was always to be far safer than humans, not just as good. Removing a cheap sensor that directly measures velocity, overruling your own engineers to do it, and ending up with a 3.2-million-vehicle NHTSA investigation into cameras that can’t tell when they’re blind isn’t first-principles engineering. It’s a position Musk staked out in 2019 when he called lidar a “fool’s errand,” and he’s been defending it ever since.

Tesla’s own behavior has drifted anyway. It’s building its own fleet maps after years of mocking them, and its Robotaxi runs inside geofences like everyone else’s. Meanwhile, Waymo, with lidar, radar, and cameras, has logged roughly 271 million rider-only miles. Tesla has about 3 million driverless miles since it started pulling safety monitors in January.

#4498. Driven: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Is the Best Nissan on Sale Today

Nissan’s e-Power hybrid powertrain transforms the Rogue into a legitimate contender for the segment’s throne.

There’s confidence, and then there’s whatever Nissan is doing. The automaker is so confident in the 2027 Rogue Hybrid that it included a fleet of hybrid Toyota RAV4s for comparison. To say this is a rare event is underselling it. But, as it turns out, Toyota (and Honda) should be on high alert. This fourth-generation Rogue is quiet, comfortable, and most of all, refined in a way that punches well above the rest of the Nissan lineup.

The new Rogue Hybrid couldn’t come at a better time for Nissan. While Toyota and Honda have both been able to sell hybrid crossovers in the hundreds of thousands each year, Nissan took a different route, most recently settling for a rebadged Mitsubishi Outlander plug-in hybrid model. However, the Rogue Hybrid has a trick up its sleeve for 2027, one that we think has real legs.

The secret behind the new Rogue’s competence is its e-Power series-hybrid powertrain. This third generation of Nissan’s multi-energy system is the first on offer in the States. The powertrain starts with a turbocharged 1.5-liter three-cylinder engine running on the Miller cycle, which serves as a generator to feed power to a compact lithium-ion battery pack. In turn, that battery sends power to a pair of electric drive motors—one on the front axle and one on the rear—giving the Rogue a full-time all-wheel-drive setup with independent motor control.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid for sale near 33486

This isn’t the same gas engine as in the brand’s other models. Nissan’s engineers told us that while the automaker does have another turbocharged 1.5-liter three-banger on the shelf, the two powerplants have little in common. For starters, the Rogue’s engine sports a larger turbocharger; one downside of bigger snails is that they take more time to spool before providing boost (and thus torque), but because the Rogue’s engine never powers the wheels, continually needing to build boost is not an issue. Nissan was able to tune the engine to spend most of its time between 2000 and 5000 rpm, which also keeps the engine’s harmonics in check and mitigates noise, vibration, and harshness.

In practice, the e-Power system is great. There are five levels of regeneration, including a true one-pedal driving mode. Thanks to the electric traction motors, Nissan developed what it calls Smooth Stop. The tech manages the final moments of deceleration to control the vehicle’s pitch and reduce any head bob when coming to a halt.

Press the right pedal, and with a combined 225 horsepower, accelerating from a stop is smooth yet perky. Nissan quotes a 60-mph time of 6.4 seconds—which would make it quicker than both the RAV4 and CR-V Hybrid—but we’ll have to wait until we can subject one to our testing regimen before we verify that figure. Even without our equipment, we can tell that the Rogue has plenty of getup. That instant e-motor torque means highway passing is a breeze. Plus, the system is zippy without giving up much in terms of fuel efficiency: The midrange SR trim earns an EPA-estimated 41 mpg city, 36 highway, and 38 combined; the SV and Platinum trims are down 1 mpg on the highway and in their combined ratings, making the Rogue not quite a class leader but not too far off either.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid for sale near 33486

On the curvy roads surrounding Santa Barbara, California, the Rogue handled itself well. The steering is a bit lifeless, but it’s no worse than the rest of the segment. Hustle the Rogue through a particularly tight curve, and the rear-axle torque vectoring will keep understeer to a minimum. We’re hesitant to speak too favorably of the Rogue’s ride quality, given the dearth of broken pavement we traversed, but we came away with no real grievances against the crossover’s suspension and high hopes for its composure over the poorly maintained roads around our home office.

The Rogue’s new interior is less impressive than its powertrain and driving demeanor, but we’ve got little to complain about. Nissan did a good job of hiding any cost-cutting here. Faux leather on the seats might be an expectation, but in here, the material extends to the door trim, center console, dashboard, and even the side of the central tunnel. Also, card-carrying members of the Piano Black Haters Club will appreciate a total lack of fingerprint magnets. The cabin is also a practical space, with up to 66 cubic feet of storage when the second row is folded down. Parents will appreciate that the rear doors open nearly 90 degrees, giving plenty of room to install or remove a car seat.

The base SV and mid-level SR trims come with a 12.3-inch touchscreen setup, though the SR model we drove was optioned with a 14.3-inch unit (standard on the Platinum) running a Google-based OS with support for wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. The resolution is crisp, and the screen is plenty responsive, but our favorite part of the cockpit is situated below the displays. There, Nissan equipped the new Rogue with dedicated physical controls for the heated and cooled seats, temperature, fan speed, and climate-control modes. The wireless phone charger located at the front of the center console includes magnets, and they work wonders to prevent your phone from sliding around like a greased pig (the Platinum trim gets dual wireless phone chargers). While we will never hate on the presence of switchgear, we do wish the array felt a bit nicer to manipulate.

We found the Rogue’s seats plenty comfortable, even after a full day of driving. Wind and tire noise are hushed, allowing for quiet conversations while keeping driving fatigue to a minimum. Still, for as mitigated as they are, wind and tire noise are more prevalent in the cabin than engine noise, which is seemingly kept under lock and key about two towns over. There’s so little engine NVH that most passengers shouldn’t notice when the turbo three-pot kicks on to power the battery.

The Rogue Hybrid is priced attractively too. Since Nissan wants the next-generation nonhybrid Rogue to serve as the model’s entry point, there’s no generic S trim for the hybrid. Instead, the electrified Rogue lineup starts at $37,065 with the SV variant. The SR (the trim we drove) will be the first trim to arrive and will start at $39,065. The SV and the $45,065 Platinum won’t arrive until January.

There’s no doubt about it: The 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid isn’t just the most compelling product in Nissan’s lineup; it’s compelling, period. You’ll notice we didn’t even bother talking about the Toyota that sat right next to it.

In the late 2000s, every car manufacturer thought the best way to boost sales was to shove a new model into every market and vehicle size they could. What happened was that some models sold well initially, but as the market matured and weeded out unnecessary, awkward segments, they eventually killed some cars.

That’s what happened to the Ford Edge; Ford believed it needed a mid-sized crossover slotted between the Escape and the 3-row Explorer. The Edge enjoyed a relatively long run in the U.S. but met its maker back in 2024.

However, the Ford Edge nameplate continues in other markets, specifically the major car market of China, where it serves as a premium 3-row SUV/Crossover for the brand. For 2027, Ford will introduce a refreshed version in China with new features and a revitalized look. Autohome published a report saying it got information from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology that the Ford Edge L is getting a host of new features and some exterior design tweaks.

Design-wise, the updated Ford Edge L gets sharper LED headlights integrated with the front grille. The chrome strip and LED DRLs have also been redesigned, and the front bumper now includes side air vents. On the sides, things remain the same, but with 3 new rim size options: 19, 20, or 21 inches. The rear now gets a roof spoiler with an integrated high-mounted brake light, and a rear wiper on the rear window. The taillights retain the continuous design with an embedded Edge logo in the center.

Inside, the 2027 Ford Edge L features a 2+2+3 seating configuration designed to resemble a first-class cabin. The seats include 14-point pneumatic massage and pneumatic leg rests, plus armrest storage. Ford also added handles to the B pillars for easier entry and exit. It also gets new tech features like the SYNC MAX intelligent connectivity system, featuring a built-in 8155 chip, a new UI interface, and CarPlay support.

Interestingly, Ford is offering the Edge L in China as a pure gasoline or hybrid vehicle. The ICE version has the standard non-electrified 2.0-liter turbocharged engine, which makes a healthy 248 hp. The hybrid version uses the same base gasoline engine but adds a hybrid system for 270 hp. The Edge L also comes in two drive versions: two-wheel-drive and four-wheel-drive.

#4496. Hyundai hints at IONIQ P as the name for its new entry-level EV

Hyundai is launching a new mass-market electric SUV to be made in India, expected to go on sale as the IONIQ P.

After disguised prototypes have been spotted testing in public several times now, we may know the name of Hyundai’s compact electric SUV.

During its third-quarter earnings call, Hyundai said it would introduce the IONIQ P in India following the new Bayon.

Although it didn’t explicitly confirm the name of the upcoming model, codenamed HE1i, it’s expected to go on sale as the IONIQ P as the latest addition to Hyundai’s dedicated IONIQ EV lineup.

Mr. Tarun Garg, Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer of Hyundai Motor India, declared on Wednesday that the “Launch of Bayon marks the onset of our golden product cycle. He added We are also fully geared up for the launch of [our] dedicated mass market EV in Q4 FY27.”

The vehicle was first spotted earlier this year driving near Hyundai’s Sriperumbudur plant in Chennai, India, the “Detroit of Asia,” as it’s known.

Hyundai has yet to confirm the name, but the vehicle carried an “HE1i” tag, suggesting it was an IONIQ model.

Previous electric test vehicles, like the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, were tagged with “ME” and “NE,” with the “E” indicating they are based on the dedicated E-GMP platform.

The new entry-level EV will sit below the Creta Electric as a smaller, lower-priced electric SUV that will serve as a cornerstone of Hyundai’s growth plans in India.

During its CEO Investor Day in August, Hyundai Motor announced plans to launch 100 new or refreshed vehicles between now and 2030, including 58 in North America, 49 in South Korea, 41 in Europe, and 26 in India.

Alongside the recently launched IONIQ 3 and new Tucson, Hyundai previewed a new electric A-SUV for India, a global B-SUV, and another B-SUV for Europe.

Hyundai Motor is investing $15.5 billion to expand its presence in India by 2032, including expanding manufacturing capacity and building a local supply chain. The new entry-level EV will be Hyundai’s first produced locally in India. By 2030, Hyundai expects total production capacity to reach 1.1 million units in India.

Hyundai’s global sales fell 10% year over year in the third quarter to 931,211 units. India, meanwhile, was its fastest-growing market with sales up 9.5% in Q3 to over 150,000 units.

Will Hyundai bring the compact electric SUV to other global markets? The company said India will serve as an “important export hub,” but didn’t offer any further details.

A covered prototype was recently caught testing in South Korea by ShortsCar, initially thought to be the IONIQ 4 or possibly IONIQ 1.

Hyundai already exports vehicles made in India to global markets like the UK, Central and South America, and the Middle East, so it wouldn’t be a surprise.

In September, Hyundai’s domestic sales and exports from India rose 11% to 77,916, the highest monthly total yet.

Bugatti CEO Chased His Stolen Chiron Across Borders in a Porsche 911

The driver simply holds the brake pedal as the system automatically adjusts braking force for a smoother stop.

Pagani Reveals Final Huayra 70 One-Off With a Manual Gearbox

Karma Reveals a 1,200-HP V8 Hybrid Built for Just One Buyer

Why Chinese Cars Are Packed With Features Americans Don't Always Ask For

Toyota GR86 Performance Pads Apparently Cost

One of the notable features in the 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid is the e-Power system, a series hybrid that uses electric motors to drive the wheels while the engine serves as a generator. As such, the compact crossover delivers an EV-like driving experience minus the range anxiety.

But aside from the smoothness of EV-like operation, Nissan is championing a new feature called Smooth Stop. Inspired by a technique known as a “limo stop,” the feature automatically reduces braking pressure just before the vehicle comes to a complete stop, minimizing the forward-and-backward jerking sensation passengers typically experience.

With Smooth Stop, drivers can simply maintain pressure on the brake pedal without manually adjusting it. Similar comfort technology has been available in BMW models like the E90-generation 3 Series, but Nissan claims Smooth Stop is a first-in-class feature, giving the Rogue Hybrid an advantage over direct rivals like the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4. Perhaps Nissan can bank on Smooth Stop to distinguish the Rogue Hybrid, especially considering it has added other comfort features.

For one, Nissan made the cabin quieter by adding sound-deadening materials in noise-prone areas like the wheel wells and reducing wind noise through concealed windshield wipers, door-mounted side mirrors, and slim roof rails. The cabin also features Zero Gravity seats, soft-touch materials, and generous front headroom that contribute to comfort, while the available ventilated front seats were redesigned to minimize operating noise. The Japanese marque claims that normal conversations can be maintained between front and rear passengers, even at highway speeds.

Another comfort feature is the improved ProPilot Assist, the brand’s advanced driver-assistance system, similar in purpose to Ford’s BlueCruise. The system comes with a new front camera with a 20% wider field of view, increased object-detection range, and improved steering control for centering the vehicle in the lane. Moreover, it is available with Hands-Off Traffic Jam Support for hands-free steering at speeds below 30 mph and Auto Lane Change, which requires the driver’s hands to remain on the wheel. The system was developed and tested in California.

While the Nissan Rogue has been the brand’s best-selling model in the U.S., its sales still trail those of its main rivals by a wide margin. In 2025, Nissan sold 217,896 Rogues, significantly fewer than the 479,288 Toyota RAV4s and 403,768 Honda CR-Vs sold. But for the 2027 model year, Nissan is switching up the formula with a new series hybrid system and a more comfortable driving experience.

How that will pan out remains to be seen. The 2027 Rogue Hybrid will arrive first in the SR AWD trim with the SR Technology Package in limited quantities in late November 2026, with a $41,490 MSRP. More affordable trims and the more expensive Platinum trim will follow in early 2027.

#4491. A Cracked Oil Pan Killed One of Porsche's Most Reliable Flat-Six Engines

Just 11% of Gas-Car Owners See an EV as Their Likely Next Buy

BMW Employs Professional Sniffers to Eliminate New Car Smell

Bugatti CEO Chased His Stolen Chiron Across Borders in a Porsche 911

The MA1.04, found in the 991.1-generation 911s, is one of the most reliable powerplants from the German marque, so a failure like this is a rather rare sight.

Used EVs Are Selling Faster Than Gas Cars, but Tesla Isn't Leadingм

Toyota Tundra Owner Dodges $25,000 Repair His Truck Didn't Actually Need

Winter Weather Advisory Issued for Up to 15 Inches of Snow and 55 MPH Gusts Today

Rare Green Ferrari Daytona SP3 Sells for $18.5 Million

In the bible of engine reliability, you need a couple of things: A proven design and architecture, proper usage cycles and care, and religious maintenance and service intervals. The Porsche MA1.04 is part of a series of internal combustion engine families from Stuttgart that is regarded as some of the brand’s most reliable powertrains it has ever produced, so for one to come into the shop for a teardown is somewhat of an event.

Even some more modern Porsches aren’t exempt from the occasional engine problem here and there. Porsche’s very quick to revise their design once a flaw is identified, but somehow, the MA1 series just got it mostly right. While not perfect, the flat-six still has a few failure points and maintenance-intensive areas that owners should know about, but none of those failure points appeared to be the culprit when this motor decided to blow.

Right off the bat, I Do Cars found the root cause. There’s a crack in the oil pan. So the engine ran without oil once the level dipped to dangerous levels, and it soon became a coffee table.

The damage done was reportedly $10,000 at the time for a new motor without labor. The engine was graciously donated by a fan of I Do Cars after being sat for a while. While the damage to the owner’s wallet is documented, the full extent of the damage to the motor and why it was replaced was only revealed towards the end of the video.

In the middle of the teardown, I Do Cars did notice a few things that were not ideal for a motor, like some shavings and fragments in the combustion chamber. That was just a teaser of things to come, however.

So after getting all the nuts and bolts out of the assembly, the engine comes apart. It’s interesting to note that the MA1 splits apart right down the middle. Once the flat six turned into two inline-threes, we get to see what went wrong. Up until this point, everything was peak German precision. However, the deeper I Do Cars dug, the more heartbreaking it ended up being.

All the rods and pistons were intact with acceptable wear, and even the rod bearings were good, but they have seen better days. That all changes, however, when the camera pointed to the main bearings. One bearing welded itself to the crankshaft, while the rest looked like it had been mangled.

That’s not the worst part, though. On one half of the block, we can see a nasty score at the crankcase. Basically, chunks of aluminum are just sitting there in a crevice. This is a bad case of a spun bearing, and it was enough to basically stop the engine dead in its tracks.

The fact that this was all caused by a hit to the oil pan makes this even more heartbreaking. Now, yes, some parts from this motor can still be reused by resourceful builders, but the block itself might be out of commission. An extremely skilled machinist might be able to repair it, but it could cost more to repair than to replace as a whole unit. Maybe the block is destined to be turned into a coffee table after all.

#4490. Rivian (RIVN) Q3 2026 earnings: revenue up 38%, R2 now its best-seller

Rivian (RIVN) just released its Q3 2026 earnings, with revenue up 38% year-over-year to $2.155 billion. The R2, in its first full quarter of deliveries, is already the company’s best-selling vehicle, ahead of both the R1 and the Amazon van.

The results beat Wall Street’s expectations, and Rivian is raising its 2026 guidance on every metric. But the car business is still losing money, and the R2 ramp made the automotive margin worse this quarter.

We already had the volume side. Rivian reported earlier this month that it built 19,751 vehicles and delivered 19,248 in the quarter, both records. Deliveries were up 46% from a year ago and 58% from Q2.

Analysts were looking for about $2.02 billion in revenue, an adjusted loss of $0.61 per share, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of roughly $576 million, according to Bloomberg consensus. Rivian beat all three.

The demand signals for the R2 are good. Rivian says reservation conversion for the launch edition trim stayed above its expectations, it added a second R2 production shift in Normal, Illinois, and demo drives jumped to over 103,000 in the quarter, up from 57,000 in Q2.

The problem is the automotive gross margin. Rivian’s automotive segment posted an $80 million gross loss in Q3, a -5% margin. That’s better than the $130 million loss a year ago, but worse than the $36 million loss (-3%) we saw in Q2.

Rivian blames about $120 million of extra cost of revenue on the R2 ramp, compared to production at “more normalized levels.” And the quarter got help that won’t repeat on demand: $81 million in regulatory credit revenue and an IEEPA tariff refund receivable.

Strip out the credits and the automotive segment lost about $161 million at the gross level, or roughly $8,400 per vehicle delivered. Not great.

But there’s real progress under that. Rivian says automotive cost of goods sold per unit fell by more than $12,000 quarter-over-quarter thanks to the higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage. Our own math from the filing puts it at about $84,700 per vehicle in Q3, down from $96,700 in Q2. Revenue per vehicle is coming down too, which is the point of a cheaper car: about $76,300 excluding credits, versus $85,000 in Q2.

The only reason Rivian posted a consolidated gross profit is its software and services segment, which brought in $605 million in revenue and $256 million in gross profit, a 42% margin.

Of that segment revenue, $354 million (59%) came from the joint venture with Volkswagen Group, which pays Rivian for electrical architecture and software development work. Rivian says it expects to recognize that revenue through about mid-2028. Autonomy+, the paid driver-assist package launched in April, is also in there, and Rivian says take rates are “trending ahead of our expectations.”

With 41,807 deliveries through September, Rivian needs between 25,193 and 28,193 in Q4 to land in the new range. That would be another record by a wide margin. Rivian is providing this guidance a month into the quarter, which gives strong confidence it will hit at leat the lower end of that target.

The capex cut is about “timing of spend,” not savings. Phase 1 of the Georgia plant, which is supposed to add 300,000 units of annual capacity for R2 and R3, is still under construction.

On cash, Rivian ended the quarter with $5.502 billion, or $7.095 billion in total liquidity once you add its credit facility and the $1 billion term loan Volkswagen funded in October. That’s after the $1.5 billion share sale in July. Free cash flow was -$1.124 billion in Q3 alone.

This is a good quarter for Rivian, and the R2 is clearly working. Becoming the best-selling Rivian within one full quarter, while the ramp is still early, is about as good a start as you could ask for. We saw the R2 roll off the line in April, and the demand side has held up since.

But be careful with the headline beat. A lot of it came from outside the car business: Volkswagen’s checks, regulatory credits, and a one-time tariff refund. The thing Rivian actually builds and sells lost more money at the gross level than it did last quarter.

Picked my R2 up a week ago and I’m already in love. It was worth the two year wait! I find myself looking for excuses to jump in and go for a joy ride.

Rivian is going to sell a metric ton of the lower cost versions.

The number we care about most is the $12,000 drop in cost per vehicle. If that keeps going as the second shift fills and the $120 million in ramp costs fade, the automotive segment can get to breakeven on its own. If it stalls, Rivian is a software contractor for VW with a money-losing car company attached.

I am betting on the former. With a shift added right before the quarter started, production will likely increase significantly in Q4, and Rivian already has strong visibility into demand a month into the quarter.

If anything, I’m impressed by the demand Rivian is seeing for the more expensive launch edition of the R2. It bodes well for the cheaper version, as long as it manages to get its cost down over the coming months.

Mitsubishi has confirmed that the all-new Pajero (or Montero as it’s known in some markets) will go on sale in Japan on December 17.

The all-new Pajero will be available in four trims in Japan: Super Exceed, Exceed, GSR, and GLS. The former two trims are more luxury oriented, while the latter two are more focused on off-road capability.

The Japanese market will get a single powertrain—a 2.4-liter turbo diesel engine rated at 201 horsepower at 3,500 rpm and 354 pound-feet of torque from 1,750 to 2,500 rpm. Mated to an 8-speed automatic transmission with Sport mode, the engine is said to return a fuel economy of 12.1 km/L on the WLTC cycle, which is the equivalent of 28.5 MPG.

The transmission sends power to all four wheels via the Super Select 4WD-II (SS4-II) system, which allows drivers to select from four modes: 2H (rear-wheel drive), 4H (full-time 4WD), 4HLc (locked center differential), and 4LLc (locked center differential with low-range gears). According to Mitsubishi, the SS4-II system combines “high off-road capability with excellent on-road handling stability.”

The AWD system is integrated into the Super-All Wheel Control (S-AWC) vehicle dynamics control system, which controls driving, cornering and braking.

S-AWC also integrates control of Active Yaw Control (AYC), which uses the front brakes to control torque between the left and right wheels, Active Stability and Traction Control (ASTC), which distributes driving force to enhance stability on slippery surfaces, and ABS.

The new Pajero offers seven selectable drive modes for specific driving conditions: Normal, Eco, Gravel, Snow, Mud, Sand and Rock. The Pajero is based on the ladder-frame chassis from the Mitsubishi Triton pickup, which is a great prerequisite for off-road capability.

Models equipped with 20-inch tires (standard on Super Exceed and Exceed trims) offer 9 inches (230 mm) of ground clearance, a 30.4-degree approach angle, a 22.6-degree ramp breakover angle, and a 25.8-degree departure angle.

The new Pajero is already on sale in Thailand and will launch in Australia later this year before expanding to around 100 other international markets. The United States has not been confirmed among those markets, but Mitsubishi previewed a body-on-frame flagship SUV to U.S. dealers under the Montero name. If the Montero does arrive stateside in the coming years it will definitely need a different powertrain to meet U.S. emissions certification.

#4488. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#4487. Toyota’s EV sales more than doubled in a year, but gas cars are getting crushed in China

Toyota’s EV sales have jumped 127% through September, but that isn’t telling the whole story. Slumping demand for gas and hybrid cars in China has pushed global sales lower for three months in a row.

Including Lexus, Toyota sold 309,766 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) globally through the first nine months of 2026, up 127.4% from the same period last year.

Except for January (+87.5%), Toyota’s EV sales have more than doubled every month this year compared with 2025.

The higher demand comes after Toyota and Lexus launched updated versions of their first-gen electric SUVs, the bZ4X (now the bZ in the US) and the RZ.

Toyota has added several new electric models, including the C-HR+ (C-HR in the US), bZ4X Touring (bZ Woodland in the US), and Urban Cruiser, while Lexus now offers the ES EV. Both brands will introduce a three-row electric SUV, which is expected to go on sale over the next few months.

According to data from Cleantechnica, the Toyota bZ4X became the 20th best-selling EV worldwide through August, with nearly 100,000 units sold.

While its EVs are catching on, Toyota Motor’s global sales fell for the third straight month in September.

Toyota sold 860,107 vehicles in September, down 2.2% from the previous year. The company said that although overall demand remained steady, sales in China fell, leading to lower overall sales than last year.

Through September, Toyota sold 7.51 million vehicles globally, down 3.4%. In China, Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20%, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales.

Toyota said the overall market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” resulting in lower sales.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Toyota sells several electric vehicles through its two joint ventures (GAC Toyota and FAW Toyota) in China, including the bZ3, bZ3X, bZ5, and bZ7.

After the US, China is Toyota’s second-largest market. Through September, Toyota has now sold more vehicles in its home market of Japan (1.19 million) than in China.

To turn things around and compete with companies like BYD, Toyota, like many major OEMs nowadays, is increasingly adopting more Chinese EV tech and manufacturing practices.

Nikkei reported in August that Toyota plans to build a new Lexus electric SUV in China, rather than in Japan as it has traditionally. Production is expected to begin at Lexus’ new manufacturing plant in Shanghai next fall.

Toyota's EV sales still represent less than 3% of its overall sales. This is the real news.

BTW, Toyota's European sales got hit in a similar way. They are up 0,7% YoY but that's compared to a rising overall market of 5,7%. This lead to it's market share shrinking.

The new Lexus EV will use advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up production.

Toyota isn’t the only legacy automaker struggling to keep pace in China’s fast-moving automotive market.

Volkswagen Group CFO and COO, Arno Antilitz, admitted the company “must act quickly and decisively” after reporting third-quarter sales in China dropped 38% to 405,800 units on Thursday. The company also plans to use technology developed in China for its next-gen EVs, which it will sell overseas.

#4484. Rivian’s electric van gets 30% more range and AWD, now delivering

Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.

The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.

Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.

Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”

EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.

The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.

The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:

Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.

So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.

200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.

The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.

The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.

Rivian needs to make the sales to USPS. I am starting to see those vans all the time now. It looks like it is designed from ground up to optimize for delivery. Extra height for drivers, lower floor of entry, great visibility in the front. Low bumper and lower headlight position for safety. Overall, great design.

Too bad that GM dropped Brightdrop van just as they are getting popular. I see a lot of FedEx trucks are now Bright drop. Perfect timing when diesel price is thru the roof. GM never have the long term view and always good at starting something but give up just before it becomes a hot seller.

This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.

Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.

The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

#4481. Used EVs Are Selling Faster Than Gas Cars or Hybrids

A recent study claims that used EVs are moving off the market much faster than gas or hybrid cars, despite higher prices.

Shoppers in the market for a used car are reportedly shifting toward electric powertrains. A report from iSeeCars claims that EVs are the quickest-moving cars in the used-car market compared with their gas and hybrid counterparts, despite a higher price point than last year.

The report studied over 1.5 million cars between one and five years old to find trends in the current used-car market. Between September 2025 and September 2026, used EVs saw a 9.8 percent price increase, while hybrid prices rose 4.9 percent and gas-powered prices rose less than half a percent. EVs sold for an average of $32,533 in September 2026, landing right in the middle of the more expensive hybrids at $34,476 and less expensive gas-powered vehicles at $31,954.

See all results for used cars for sale near 70810

Though EV prices are increasing, they’re moving off sales floors a lot faster than gasoline models that have stayed relatively the same price. In September 2026, used EVs averaged 41.9 days on the market, which is 13 days less than gas-powered cars. Hybrids find themselves in the middle with about 48.6 days on the market. Compared with September 2025, used EVs sold 10.1 percent faster, while gas cars saw a 19.9 percent longer sales window.

However, gas-powered cars take up the top two spots on the overall fastest-selling cars list. The Lexus IS500, which saw its last production year in 2025, took the top spot, followed by the Audi A4 Allroad, another gasoline model. The Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback sits in third place as the first EV on the list, spending an average of 29.8 days on the market. Gas-powered cars may have dominated the top two spots, but EVs still managed to sell faster overall than the gas-powered herd.

The fastest-selling EVs recorded were the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron, followed by the Toyota bZ4X, and the Lexus RZ 300e. Though not on the top-10 fastest-selling list at all, Teslas saw some of the highest price increases this year, with the Model S averaging $10,636 higher than in September 2025 and the Model X gaining $9336. The Model 3’s price increased by about $3870.

EV prices started rising in April 2026 and have steadily increased since then, reaching a peak in August. As gas prices continue to soar in the United States, it appears more people are interested in going electric. When used-car shoppers aren’t looking at electric models, luxury brands tend to sell better than more mainstream models.

#4479. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4478. What If Your Car's Brakes Fail? Bosch Has a Touchscreen Solution

Bugatti CEO Chased His Stolen Chiron Across Borders in a Porsche 911

Bosch’s latest patent explores how drivers could retain braking control even after an electronic system failure.

Rare Green Ferrari Daytona SP3 Sells for $18.5 Million

Pagani Reveals Final Huayra 70 One-Off With a Manual Gearbox

Karma Reveals a 1,200-HP V8 Hybrid Built for Just One Buyer

Why Chinese Cars Are Packed With Features Americans Don't Always Ask For

Brake-by-wire isn’t some sci-fi fantasy anymore. It’s already here, with plenty of new cars ditching old-school cables and rods for sensors, computers, and electronic gizmos. Instead of a direct link between your foot and the brakes, the car now reads your pedal press and decides how hard to clamp down –  all through electronics.

However, this approach also raises an important question: What happens when the electronics responsible for stopping your car fail?

Bosch thinks it has a solution. The company just filed a patent for a backup braking system that steps in when the main electronics go on vacation. Basically, it’s an extra safety net that could let you bring your car to a stop even if the usual tech throws in the towel.

First spotted by CarMoses, the patent describes a system that uses three separate control units. The first and second handle the vehicle’s regular braking operations, while the third continuously monitors them for potential failures.

If the third control unit detects that either of the other units has malfunctioned, it can activate an emergency braking function. It can also notify the driver through visual, audible, or haptic warnings.

What’s particularly interesting is how Bosch proposes allowing the driver to request braking. Rather than relying exclusively on a conventional brake pedal, the system could provide an emergency button through the vehicle’s infotainment touchscreen. Another proposed implementation places the control directly on the steering wheel, where it’s easier to reach without taking your hands off the wheel.

You might even get to control how hard you stop – hold the button for more braking, tap for less. Bosch says you could ease into a stop instead of slamming to a halt, which sounds nice in theory.

This makes the concept different from a conventional automatic emergency braking system, which generally intervenes to avoid or mitigate a collision. Bosch’s proposal instead focuses on giving drivers an alternative braking interface when the regular electronic controls become unavailable.

With more brands jumping on the brake-by-wire bandwagon, having a backup brain and a new way to hit the brakes could be a smart move if the electronics ever flake out.

But let’s be real: in a panic, hunting for a virtual brake button on a screen sounds like a recipe for chaos. A button on the steering wheel might make more sense, but it’s still a far cry from stomping on a pedal. For now, this is just a patent, not a promise. Like plenty of wild ideas before it, there’s no guarantee it’ll ever make it into your next car.

#4477. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4476. Arc Raiders gets a few map exploit fixes in latest patch as Embark prepares to slow down how often patches are released

There's a new Arc Raiders patch that's fairly small, but one with fixes everyone is going to appreciate.

The time has arrived for another Arc Raiders update, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more important than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

Starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

On Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision issue that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

The last change in this update affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Alongside today’s patch, Embark also announced that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it launched in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

But, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more big update. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

#4474. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

Up to 18 inches of snow is forecast above 10,000 feet under winter storm warnings from the National Weather Service, with the first warning beginning at 8 a.m. ET Sunday and gusts reaching 50 mph. Forecasters say travel could become very difficult to impossible in blowing and drifting snow, and the warnings hold until 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. ET Monday, past the Monday morning commute.

The NWS Grand Junction winter storm warning for the northwest and southwest San Juan Mountains is already in effect and runs until 2 p.m. ET Monday. It calls for 12 to 18 inches above 10,000 feet, with locally higher amounts and gusts to 45 mph. The office upgraded it from a winter storm watch on Saturday morning. Telluride, Ouray, Silverton, Lake City, Rico and Hesperus are inside it, along with Red Mountain, Molas, Coal Bank and Lizard Head passes.

Farther east, NWS Pueblo has the eastern San Juan Mountains above 10,000 feet under a warning from 7 p.m. ET Sunday to 1 p.m. ET Monday, covering Wolf Creek Pass and Cumbres Pass. It forecasts 8 to 14 inches and the strongest wind of the storm, with gusts to 50 mph that could produce areas of blowing and drifting snow. Pueblo expects the worst travel Sunday night and Monday morning.

Colorado is not the only state on the alert map this weekend. NWS offices also have winter alerts posted in Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, Nevada and California, including a winter storm warning for the Ruby Mountains in Nevada.

Wolf Creek Pass carries US 160 over the eastern San Juans. According to the Colorado Department of Transportation, the road drops at a 7 percent grade for more than eight miles from the summit, with a hairpin curve six and a half miles down and two runaway truck ramps along the way.

CDOT’s Wolf Creek guidance for truck drivers advises checking the brakes before descending, maintaining a low speed in a low gear, and not riding the brakes, which can cause overheating. The summit’s wide shoulder doubles as a chain-up area for traffic in both directions.

On US 550, Red Mountain Pass runs below avalanche terrain. In 2023 CDOT installed remote avalanche control systems at slide paths on the pass, two Gazex units and three O’bellx units that use compressed air and gases to trigger controlled avalanches above the road while it is closed. CDOT says crews can run that work in the early morning, before commuter traffic builds, and that the systems shorten closures.

Across the state, CDOT and the Colorado Avalanche Information Center monitor 522 avalanche paths above state highways and I-70, with active mitigation on 278 of them. Colorado’s road conditions are on COtrip and through 511.

The mechanicals are nearly identical, the Quartermaster using the same BMW-sourced 281-hp turbocharged inline-six, eight-speed automatic transmission, solid axles, and four-wheel drive system as the wagon. While its retro-Rover styling could be construed as pretentious, its 1840-pound payload capacity and 7716-pound tow rating tell a different story.
