#4442. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

Building a massive automotive assembly plant from scratch is a monumental financial gamble, but the strategic joint venture between Mazda and Toyota is officially paying off. Just five years after the very first crossover rolled off the line, Mazda Toyota Manufacturing (MTM) in Huntsville, Alabama, is celebrating the production of its one-millionth vehicle. The sprawling domestic facility currently splits its enormous production capacity between two highly popular compact crossovers: the rugged Mazda CX-50 and the sensible Toyota Corolla Cross.

Reaching this seven-figure production milestone is a massive achievement for the 4,500 team members working at the Alabama plant. It proves that despite supply chain volatility and rapidly shifting consumer demands, domestic manufacturing remains incredibly viable when major automakers successfully pool their resources.

Massive manufacturing facilities often have a strained relationship with the local communities they occupy. Too often, we see headlines about aggressive factory construction expansions severely disrupting long-time residents and transforming quiet neighborhoods. However, MTM utilized its one-millionth vehicle celebration as a direct opportunity to actively invest in the surrounding Huntsville area. The automaker announced $120,000 in local grant funding specifically dedicated to the educational organizations that supported their workforce development.

Recipients of the grant include Calhoun Community College, Kids to Love, Morgan County Schools, and the Alabama Automotive Manufacturer’s Association. This localized investment aligns perfectly with Toyota’s overarching domestic strategy, as the Japanese giant is continuously spending massive capital to solidify its manufacturing footprint across the United States.

From an editorial perspective, this production milestone is critical for both brands, but it carries far more weight for Mazda. While Toyota has an absolutely massive global manufacturing network to rely on, Mazda’s ultimate survival in the highly competitive North American market depends heavily on this specific partnership. Sharing development and production costs allows the smaller automaker to punch significantly above its weight class without going bankrupt.

By actively investing in the local workforce and successfully churning out a million in-demand crossovers, MTM has established a blueprint for modern automotive joint ventures. Having a reliable, high-volume production facility firmly planted on American soil will give both brands a distinct competitive advantage for decades to come.

#4440. Arc Raiders' latest patch adds two of the most requested features, but kills Cred hoarding

The last major Arc Raiders update of the year has arrived, bringing several big new features to the game, but not without some bad news.

Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere. This is a significant patch for the extraction shooter for a number of reasons, not least of which because it kicks off a series of events under the Cold Snap banner, which introduces a new conditions to the game’s maps.

Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.

To start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights. This is especially relevant for PC players, most of whom play shooters with an ADS toggle, rather than hold. Another often requested feature has been the ability to reset the game’s skill tree.

This is now available for the cost of 2,000 Coins per skill point. It goes without saying that you’re going to need a whole lot of money to reset the entire thing, but it’s a useful option to have when you want to alter your path.

The next change is one that’s going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Arc Raiders now has a soft Cred cap of 800. This is now clearly shown on your Wallet screen, and the developer said the cap is necessary to prevent players from using their accumulated Cred to unlock new Raider Decks immediately after release.

The good news is that this won’t affect the Cred you may already have, but going forward, 800 is the most you can hold at any point. You’ll also notice that Shani has more stuff for you to buy with Cred, in case you want another way to spend what you have.

Patch 1.7.0 also brings a few other additions - and makes some changes - that are worth highlighting. You can now customise your Raider Tool, which likely means we’re going to see Raider Tool cosmetics going forward.

Speaking of items, the Aphelion weapon blueprint has been moved to Stella Montis, so you won’t be able to get it from taking down the Matriarch. The Bettina, and Rattler have both seen some balance changes.

The Bettina’s durability will now degrade a lot slower per shot, making it take 26 magazines to fully deplete durability. The base magazine size has been increased to 22, and the reload time has been cut to 4.5 seconds. Embark says this should make the weapon more viable in PvP, while also allowing it to stand on its own without the need for players bring a secondary weapon.

As for the Rattler, the only change it gets is an increase to its magazine size from 10 to 12. The idea is to make it about as effective as a Stitcher or Kettle at close ranges when it comes to PvP encounters.

And, of course, it wouldn’t be a big Arc Raiders patch without some tweaks to the game’s Arc enemies. This time, the Shredder gets all the love. The menacing unit now moves faster, turns more sharply and doesn’t get knocked back as much when shot.

The Shredder’s head now has more health, too, meaning you won’t be able to shoot it off early and confuse it. In general, the Arc unit should be smarter, especially when navigating narrow spaces. Finally, the Shredder now activates faster upon detecting (and being attacked by) players.

Beyond that, the main menu has seen a few changes to highlight ongoing events, make certain announcements quieter, make it easier to track Raider Quests and more. There’s a lot more in this update, too, such as changes to footstep loudness, several tweaks to loot and the value of certain items, and more besides. You’ll find the full change log on the official website.

Subaru has carved out a loyal following in the US, one of its biggest strongholds outside Japan. But the brand clearly thinks it’s just getting started.

According to its 2026 Integrated Report, Subaru is eyeing a 5% share of the US car market. That’s a big leap from 3.9% at the end of 2025, and it’ll take more than just keeping the current fanbase happy. Subaru wants to plug the holes in its lineup and win over drivers of all ages, coast to coast. It’s a bold move for a brand that’s usually stuck to its niche. The automaker’s challenge now is to cast a wider net without losing the quirky charm that made it a household name in the first place.

Subaru’s game plan is to roll out more models and make its factories quick on their feet. The idea is to fill in the lineup gaps and give shoppers more reasons to take a second look. Subaru’s also got its sights set on selling over 1.2 million cars a year worldwide by the early 2030s. That’s a big jump from the 896,000 it managed during the fiscal year that ended March 2026.

According to the company, flexible production is key here. Subaru’s Yajima plant in Japan started cranking out battery-electric cars in early 2026, and now the same line can build Toyota EVs right next to gas-powered Foresters.

Come fall 2026, that plant will also be churning out Subaru Forester SUVs for the US, backing up Subaru’s Indiana factory. That should help Subaru keep up when demand spikes or the market throws a curveball.

Subaru’s also sharpening its pencil with the Cost Innovation 20-30 plan, aiming to slash about ¥200 billion ($1.26 billion) a year from its expenses by 2030. That extra cash could help cushion the blow from rising costs and those pesky US tariffs.

Subaru’s already got a strong identity in America, but snagging 5% of the market means luring in folks who’ve never given the brand a second thought. That might mean jumping into segments where the competition is already throwing elbows. At this point, Subaru’s been making changes to its pricing, with base models being reintroduced for the 2027 model, lowering the price of entry.

Subaru has to walk a fine line: attract new fans without alienating the loyalists. Just tossing more models into the mix won’t cut it if they don’t bring something special to the table. Its production changes and cost-cutting efforts are sensible steps, particularly as automakers face pressure from tariffs and shifting demand. However, the bigger challenge will be making the lineup relevant to a wider audience.

Subaru knows what it wants and has a roadmap to get there. Whether it can actually poach buyers from the big names will come down to the cars it rolls out and how well they click with American drivers.

McMurtry Automotive is officially celebrating its tenth anniversary, and the high-performance world is far better for it. What began in 2016 as a tiny team of ambitious engineers in rural Gloucestershire, England, has transformed into the manufacturer of arguably the most violent and capable track car ever conceived. Over the last decade, the boutique brand expanded to nearly 100 employees and recently opened a state-of-the-art production facility in the Cotswolds, proving that a small, independent automaker can still disrupt the global hypercar establishment.

The company’s original goal was simple but seemingly impossible: build the ultimate lightweight driver’s vehicle. When their initial superbike-on-four-wheels concept didn’t commercially pan out, the late engineering pioneer and co-founder Sir David McMurtry offered a delightfully blunt solution to solve their traction limitations: “just suck it to the ground.” Inspired by banned 1970s racing technology, the team pivoted to fan-based downforce, creating a platform that would fundamentally change the performance landscape.

By engineering a proprietary “Downforce on Demand” system, McMurtry created a vehicle that literally vacuums itself to the tarmac. Twin electric fans pull air from underneath the chassis, generating a staggering 4,400 pounds of downforce while the vehicle sits at a complete standstill. This allows the almost production-ready electric drivetrain to deploy its 1,000 horsepower instantly, launching the ultra-lightweight carbon fiber chassis from zero to 60 mph in a brain-scrambling 1.55 seconds.

While Tesla promises their upcoming Roadster will use cold-gas thrusters to literally blow the competition away, McMurtry took the exact opposite approach; they built a hypercar that simply sucks. The on-track results of this extreme vacuum engineering have been nothing short of historic. The Spéirling shattered the outright hillclimb record at the Goodwood Festival of Speed in 2022, then smashed the long-standing Top Gear Test Track record. It generates so much instantaneous cornering grip that it even leaves veteran racing drivers speechless, with extreme sports legend Travis Pastrana claiming it is the fastest they’ve driven.

After a decade of relentless prototyping and high-speed testing, the pure fan car is finally transitioning from a wild concept into a tangible reality for well-heeled enthusiasts. Production of the Spéirling PURE is officially underway at the brand’s new UK facility, with the very first customer deliveries slated to begin later this year. Production is strictly capped at just 100 units worldwide, ensuring the vehicle remains an incredibly rare sight at local track days.

From an editorial perspective, McMurtry’s ten-year journey is a massive victory for independent automotive engineering. In an era where legacy manufacturers are constantly adding weight and complexity to their vehicles, McMurtry took a massive financial risk to build a pure, single-seat track weapon. Access to this unparalleled, Formula 1-level performance obviously comes at an astronomical cost, carrying a massive $1.3 million sticker before personalization. However, for the lucky few who can afford it, they are buying a literal piece of physics-defying history.

One of the few mid-size electric SUVs with a third row, the Kia EV9 shares this distinction with its cousin, the Hyundai Ioniq 9. The Kia EV9 beat it to market by two model years, however, and continues to deliver the same family-friendly experience and unique styling that make it one of our favorites in the segment.Numerous trims from the base single-motor, rear-wheel-drive Light to the twin-motor, all-wheel-drive GT-line offer EPA-estimated ranges of 230 to 305 miles and charging speeds up to 230 kW via a NACS (North American Charging Standard) port. All offer a fully modern interior, a choice of six- or seven-passenger configurations, and a decent blend of ride and handling.

Compare the 2027 Kia EV9 with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

The Wind trim now sports black 19-inch wheels, gloss-black exterior trim, and it can now be spec’d with Wolf Gray exterior paint. The Land trim gets the gloss-black wheels and exterior trim bits and a blacked-out interior from the discontinued Nightfall Edition. The Nightshade’s torque-boost function, which temporarily increases torque from 443 to 516 pound-feet, also joins the Land trim’s list of standard features.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The EV9 lineup starts with the rear-wheel-drive Light trim, which features a single rear-mounted electric motor that makes 215 horsepower. The Light Long Range version is rear-drive too. However, despite adding a bigger battery, its peak power drops to 201 horsepower. All-wheel-drive models have a dual-motor arrangement with a combined 379 ponies, and an available Boost mode increases the peak torque output to 516 pound-feet to provide quicker acceleration. We've found the EV9 to be as pleasant to drive as it is to look at. On the highway, the EV9 has a pleasingly soft ride, and while its weight is obvious, it navigates the urban landscape without burden.

In Comparison: The Hyundai Ioniq 9 AWD did the 60-mph sprint in 4.4 seconds.

The base EV9 Light and Light Long Range models are rated to tow 1000 pounds, or 2000 when equipped with trailer brakes. The Wind, Land, and GT-Line models increase those limits to 1653 and 3500 pounds, respectively, but the latter two can go as high as 5000 pounds when a proper weight-distributing hitch is in use.

In Comparison: The Hyundai Ioniq 9 AWD with the tow package is rated to tow the same 5000 pounds as the Ioniq 9, while the Jeep Wagoneer S EV and Chevrolet Blazer EV RS with RWD max out at 3500 pounds.

The entry-level Light model comes with a 76.1-kWh battery pack which offers an EPA-estimated 230 miles of driving range. At the other end of the spectrum, the Light Long Range model with the larger 99.8-kWh pack is rated by the EPA for up to 305 miles of driving per charge, while the Wind e-AWD and Land e-AWD models are rated for 283 miles. Going with the top-spec GT-line trim drops the estimated range to 280 miles per charge. During our 75-mph highway range test, the EV9 GT-Line traveled 240 miles.

Every EV9 uses Kia's 800-volt electrical architecture, allowing DC fast chargers to replenish the battery quickly. Its 230-kW maximum DC fast-charging speed is said to add 100 miles of driving range in just 13 minutes, with an average charging speed of 139 kilowatts between a 10 and 90 percent state of charge. This rate is among the highest averages of any EVs we've tested. The EV9's 11-kW on-board charger is about average among competitors.

The EPA estimates that the EV9 Long Range rear-wheel drive will return 100 MPGe in the city, 78 MPGe highway, and 89 MPGe in combined driving. The EV9 GT-Line is the least efficient, EPA-rated for 83 MPGe city, 72 MPGe highway, and 78 MPGe in combined driving. When we took the GT-Line on our 75-mph highway fuel economy route, we recorded 76 MPGe. For more information about the EV9's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

MPGe stands for miles per gallon of gas equivalent, an EPA metric that estimates PHEV and EV fuel efficiency.

In Comparison: The Hyundai Ioniq 9, with which the EV9 shares much of its DNA, offers a tiny improvement in efficiency, bettering the EV9 by one or two MPGe in most measures.

First Row: Interior material quality is excellent, with soft synthetic leather upholstery and unique mesh headrests. The underlying construction is also reassuringly sturdy, adding to the refined and luxurious cabin.

Second Row: The EV9 can be equipped either with a second-row bench for seven-passenger capacity or captain’s chairs for six-passenger capacity. The second-row captain's chairs feel much like the fronts and offer heating, ventilation, and massaging.

Third Row: In the very back, the third row easily accommodates adults but requires some concessions by those in the second row to offer comfortable legroom. On the EV9's upper trim levels, the third row is power folding.

Cargo Capacity: The EV9's rear cargo space holds 20 cubic feet, nearly as much as the Telluride, or up to 82 cubic feet with both the second and third rows folded flat. We managed to fit five carry-on bags behind the third row and 17 with the third row stowed.

Inside the EV9 is a pair of 12.3-inch screens—one for the gauge cluster and a second for infotainment—with a dedicated HVAC readout between them. The EV9 has fewer physical knobs and buttons than other Kias on sale today; just a few key HVAC controls and a volume knob remain, along with touch-sensitive controls embedded in the dash to jump between key infotainment features. Menus are logically organized, and the system further benefits from quick responses and attractive graphics. The placement of the on-screen climate controls obscures them behind the steering wheel and can be distracting to adjust while driving. Thankfully, once set, we rarely needed to make further adjustments. Two 12-volt power ports and a single 120-volt household outlet are standard.

The EV9 comes with several standard driver-assistance features, including systems such as blind-spot monitoring and automated emergency braking. Kia also offers a hands-free driving mode that's bundled with a more advanced version of adaptive cruise control. However, it's only for the EV9 GT-Line.

For information about the EV9’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

#4434. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

The Cybercab might be a robotaxi, but some of its hardware is coming to cars you can actually buy. In a bid to simplify building and powering its cars, Tesla is looking to incorporate certain components designed for its Cybercab in its passenger vehicles.

According to Drive Tesla Canada, Nick Verzini, Tesla’s head of drive unit engineering, said on a Munro Live factory tour that a new printed circuit board assembly and power stage will enter Model 3 production in 2026. They come from the inverter Tesla designed for the Cybercab it has started building.

The inverter turns the battery’s DC power into AC that spins the motor, so it affects efficiency and cost. Verzini said the new design has substantially fewer electronic components than the current Model 3 inverter, though no figure was given, and it accepts parts from multiple suppliers. When asked whether the whole unit could fit a Model Y drive unit, he said: “We kept the entire interface.” Tesla hasn’t announced a Model Y change as yet.

Don’t expect a range jump. According to reports, efficiency, range, and price figures remain the same. What fewer parts and multiple suppliers could mean, though Tesla hasn’t promised it, is simpler and cheaper-to-build cars, with less exposure to supply chain volatility. For the Cybercab, Tesla’s 2025 Impact Report reportedly targets at least 6.1 miles per kWh, an efficiency figure that is crucial for a car meant to run all day.

Not everything carries over. The Cybercab’s front-mounted motor uses an 11:1 gear ratio, versus about 9:1 in many other Teslas, and swaps the electric oil pump for a mechanical one. Motor cooling channels also move into a cheaper aluminium housing. Those changes aren’t confirmed for other models. The real test is whether or not these changes will result in real-world gains in reliability, pricing, and/or efficiency.

#4432. Peterbilt makes it easier than ever for government fleets to go electric

Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.

The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5-8 commercial trucks. That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt. “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”

I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.

See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars (regardless of what you saw on Fox News). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.

Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time, publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.

In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”

#4431. It’s official: Battlefield 6 is 2025's best-selling game, but Black Ops 7 still managed to be November’s top-seller

2025 will be remembered for many things, but in the ultra-competitive games industry, it’s going to be thought of as the year Battlefield 6 did what many thought couldn’t happen.

Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated. For one, November is always one of the most lucrative for the games industry, but this year in particular has seen several major hits - including new entries in two rival series.

We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series. The decades-old fight to claim the top spot has long been won by Call of Duty, but the latest Battlefield has achieved what many thought was impossible.

Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S. November 2025 saw spending fall by 4% compared to November 2024, bringing in a total of $5.9 billion.

Software technically saw growth during the month, but declines in hardware, and accessories were mainly responsible for the drop in overall spending. Black Ops 7 continued Call of Duty’s 18-Year Streak in topping sales in its launch month.

However, this year’s game did not also top the year-to-date charts, something the series has done consistently, and more than any other top-selling game each year - with rare exceptions. Battlefield 6 is firmly in the lead there, cementing its claim as 2025’s best-selling title. Black Ops 7, fittingly, occupies in the #7 spot there.

Separately from the best-selling game title fight, November has actually been one of the worst for the industry in terms of hardware sales. The report notes that the three major platform holders - Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo have all seen their hardware sales decline.

Spending on hardware during November amounted to only $695 million, a massive 27% decline compared to November 2024. According to the report, that’s the worst dollar amount total for any November since 2005, when it comes to hardware specifically. All three current-gen consoles totaled 1.6 million units sold, which Circana also notes is the lowest for any November since 1995.

This all doesn’t bode especially well for the industry. November has always been a key holiday shopping month, but it’s clear the constantly rising console prices - and already high game prices - have had a big impact.

Leaving your keys inside an unlocked vehicle is always a terrible idea, but doing so with a multi-million-dollar hypercar is a uniquely expensive gamble. Bugatti Rimac CEO Mate Rimac recently learned this lesson the hard way after a rather brazen car thief managed to steal his personal Bugatti Chiron directly from a company facility in Croatia. The incident unfolded casually, with security footage showing the suspect smoking a cigarette before wandering into the building, spotting the keys sitting inside the seven-figure machine, and simply driving off.

According to Rimac, he had developed a habit of leaving the keys inside his vehicles, perhaps to avoid the hassle of getting locked out. He likely assumed no one would be foolish enough to steal something so recognizable. Fortunately, an eagle-eyed employee quickly spotted the 1,479-horsepower hypercar speeding away from the factory and immediately alerted the rest of the team through a company group chat, confirming that an unauthorized joyride was indeed in progress.

We caught the drama as it happened on his Instagram page. Rather than simply sitting around and waiting for the authorities to handle the situation, the Bugatti CEO took matters into his own hands. Rimac immediately jumped behind the wheel of a nearby Porsche 911 that fortunately had a full tank of gas and began chasing down the suspect. While the thief already had roughly an hour head start and was actively fleeing toward Slovenia, Rimac had a massive technological advantage: the Chiron’s advanced live telemetry system.

This built-in factory software allowed Rimac and his engineering team to monitor the hypercar’s location, vehicle speed, and exact fuel level in real time. They continuously relayed these live updates to the police via their group chat, effectively turning the stolen Bugatti into an incredibly expensive tracking device. We wonder whether the stolen vehicle was Rimac’s notoriously high-mileage Chiron, though the executive was just relieved the situation remained under digital surveillance as the chase crossed international borders.

The cross-country pursuit finally came to an end after the thief crossed into Austria. The suspect had even stopped to put roughly half a tank of gas into the thirsty quad-turbo, 8.0-liter W16 engine, and naturally, he drove off without paying the fuel bill. Thanks to the constant barrage of live telemetry updates provided by Rimac’s team, Austrian police were eventually able to seamlessly intercept the stolen hypercar.

Fortunately, the Chiron only sustained very minor front bumper damage, avoiding the catastrophic wreckage that easily could have occurred. While I’m sure he must be glad it wasn’t his dream car, a V10-swapped BMW E30, the multi-million-dollar scare prompted an immediate policy change. The CEO has officially vowed to never leave keys inside his vehicles again, putting an end to his trusting factory habits.

#4429. Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think

For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.

It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.

And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.

The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.

For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.

Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.

The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.

You can show someone like that an electric motorcycle with better acceleration, lower maintenance costs, cheaper operating expenses, and the convenience of charging at home, and they still won’t want it.

Not because the electric motorcycle isn’t good enough, but because it isn’t what they love.

And that’s fine. There’s nothing wrong with loving gasoline motorcycles if that’s your thing. But it means that trying to convert those riders may be a losing battle, at least on any meaningful timeline.

Unfortunately though, it seems many years were wasted on that approach. Take Harley-Davidson, for example.

The brand started building its first electric motorcycle over a decade ago – commendable among all the other legacy motorcycle manufacturers that turned their noses up at the thought of going electric. When it was released in 2018, the Harley-Davidson LiveWire received rave reviews, but it just didn’t sell well. For one, it was insanely expensive at $30,000. But the other major reason was that no matter how amazing it was, it wasn’t going to scratch that gasoline itch that most riders still had.

That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line. And this brings us to how electric motorcycles will really replace their gasoline counterparts.

Now consider what’s happening with younger riders today.

Millions of people are growing up riding electric bicycles, electric scooters, and increasingly powerful e-motos. For them, electric two-wheelers aren’t some strange new alternative to the real thing. They are the real thing.

They’ve grown accustomed to instant torque, quiet operation, and the simplicity of twisting a throttle and going. To these riders, a gasoline-powered motorcycle is laughably primitive. It’d be like me handing you a gasoline-powered drill or blender. Yeah, exactly. Now look who’s suddenly on team battery, eh?

So now we have a whole new generation of riders getting ready to come of age. And eventually, many of those riders are going to want something more.

Maybe they’ve spent years riding a 28 mph electric bike, or a 40 mph electric moto. Now they’re young adults, they want to ride on faster roads, and they want something capable of 70 or 80 mph that’s actually street legal. They’ve gone from a sixteen-year-old in a hoodie to a twenty-six-year-old in a collared shirt. Instead of getting to high school, now they’re getting to work. But they haven’t lost that desire to ride.

It’s not because they’ve carefully compared electric and gasoline motorcycles and decided that electric is superior. It’s not because they’re trying to save the planet or reduce their maintenance costs. It’s simply because they grew up with electric two-wheelers as the norm.

It’s simply the next logical step in the type of riding they’ve already been doing for years.

Will a few of them transition over to gasoline-powered motorcycles? Sure. But for most, gasoline motorcycles will never even enter the equation.

Don’t get me wrong, we haven’t seen the last of gasoline motorcycles.

And I don’t even think electric motorcycles are going to suddenly outsell gasoline motorcycles because they become objectively better machines. At least not in the traditional recreational motorcycle markets we’re talking about here.

Instead, I think we’re going to see a somewhat more gradual generational transition.

Today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts will largely keep riding gasoline motorcycles. They’ll keep buying them, maintaining them, and enjoying them for as long as they can.

But as those riders age out of motorcycling, the next generation won’t replace them with another generation of gasoline motorcycle buyers. In other words, gasoline motorcycles will die out with their riders.

Increasingly, those younger riders will have already entered the world of powered two-wheelers through electric bikes and e-motos. When they’re ready to move up, electric motorcycles will be waiting for them.

And over those next few years, the technology will only become better. The only remaining Achilles’ heel of electric motorcycles – their run time – will get better and better as battery technology improves and we move towards solid-state batteries.

Suddenly they’ll be on par with gasoline motorcycles for range and ‘fueling’ time, yet will beat those combustion bikes elsewhere. But at that point, “better” won’t even matter anymore as electrics will be the only comfortable option for the vast majority of new riders. Again, you wouldn’t buy a power drill that runs on a gasoline engine when you’ve seen how convenient and effective a lithium-ion power drill has been your whole life.

Over time, the traditional gasoline motorcycle market will simply shrink as its existing customer base gets older, while electric motorcycles build an entirely new customer base alongside it.

And again, there will be exceptions in both directions. Some lifelong gasoline riders will enthusiastically embrace electric motorcycles, and some younger riders will still discover the appeal of combustion engines and running through the gears.

Living in SE Asia this all sounds very strange. The vast majority of the worlds bikes are not owned as toys, they are the main form of transport for the family. I agree with a lot of the article but Asia is already years ahead. The fuel shortages and sky high prices are pushing people electric far faster than riders are "aging out"

But the broader trend will be driven less by conversion and more by generational replacement.

That’s why electric motorcycles will eventually become the standard, even if they never manage to convince most of today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts to switch.

Gasoline motorcycles won’t necessarily disappear because electric motorcycles finally beat them at their own game. They’ll fade because the next generation of riders will be playing a different game entirely.

In other words, and to paraphrase T. S. Eliot, gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang, but with a whimper.

#4427. Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.

If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

I like the idea of a faster LSV, maybe able to cruise at 40 mph. Not a good idea for freeways but suitable for almost all urban and suburban streets. For some a better option than a bike as an urban or second vehicle.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.

It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.

Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

#4426. BMW Employs Professional Sniffers to Eliminate New Car Smell

BMW Employs Professional Sniffers to Eliminate New Car Smell

Bugatti CEO Chased His Stolen Chiron Across Borders in a Porsche 911

BMW’s odor specialists sniff everything from leather to adhesives, and the goal isn’t a pleasant fragrance. It’s a neutral cabin.

Kia Says Too Much Technology Is Taking the Fun Out of Driving

Ferrari's Brand Value Jumps 14.7% While Toyota And Tesla Fall

Ferrari Challenge Stradale Is Reportedly Returning After 20-Plus Years

Aston Martin Has Lost $3.1 Billion Since Stroll Took Over

That “new car smell” you love is actually a cocktail of chemicals, and BMW has a team of trained sniffers working to get rid of it. Why? It’s because that new-car smell comes from volatile organic compounds evaporating out of hundreds of synthetic parts in a freshly delivered vehicle.

According to BMWBlog, the automaker’s “nose team” works alongside specialized labs to judge how cabin materials really smell. Odor labs have operated in Munich since 1999 and in Shenyang, China, since 2014. Materials go into heated chambers that mimic a hot cabin, and the air is analyzed for compounds, then judged by evaluators against reference standards. The checks come in three stages: single materials, larger parts such as seats and headliners, and finally the complete vehicle, since materials can smell different in combination, especially as temperatures rise. Nils Hesse, BMW’s VP of Product Sustainability, put it this way: “A car doesn’t exist in a lab, but with its occupants.”

Unless you’re buying a BMW, it means nothing. But the science is interesting, and it claims that heat is the enemy. According to the working theory, summer sun raises cabin emissions, while overnight winter parking lowers them. BMW says newer microfiber materials cut emissions and avoid animal-derived proteins, which can cause odor as natural leather ages. Personally, I drive a W123 Mercedes, and the smell of old animal biologics in the upholstery is what sets the scene. In epic contrast, the Neue Klasse iX3 also gets a multi-stage Nano Filter to make sure you’re really only breathing the cleanest, crispest, and most premium air. As for the rest of us, if your car has a smell today, the usual advice applies: crack the windows and park in the shade. If you follow this advice with a new car, the compounds fade by roughly 20 percent a week, so the smell eases over the first few months.

Some of those compounds, like benzene and formaldehyde, are classified as human carcinogens, though typical cabin levels aren’t considered a serious hazard. The U.S. has no federal rules for in-car air, while China requires chemical tests before sale. BMW’s pitch to new car buyers is that a cabin that smells like nothing is a cabin that’s working.

#4425. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

#4423. Just 11% of Gas-Car Owners See an EV as Their Likely Next Buy

Just 11% of Gas-Car Owners See an EV as Their Likely Next Buy

BMW Employs Professional Sniffers to Eliminate New Car Smell

Bugatti CEO Chased His Stolen Chiron Across Borders in a Porsche 911

America’s EV market has progressed in recent years, but convincing traditional car buyers to switch remains a challenge.

Porsche Is Exploring a Way to Silence the Engine Drone in EVs

Ferrari F50 With Just 106 Miles Sells for a Record $17 Million

Kia Says Too Much Technology Is Taking the Fun Out of Driving

Ferrari's Brand Value Jumps 14.7% While Toyota And Tesla Fall

America’s EV market has made progress, but convincing traditional car buyers to switch remains difficult. As we’ve discussed before, electrification depends on more than adding vehicles to dealership lots. Charging access, affordability, and consumer confidence also shape demand.

A study from HERE Technologies and SBD Automotive puts that challenge into perspective. Its extensive report found that just 11% of surveyed US owners of gasoline and diesel vehicles consider an EV as their most likely next purchase or lease. The result suggests that growing infrastructure and wider model availability have yet to translate into strong buying intent.

The study surveyed 4,058 drivers across eight markets and found a difference between current EV owners and people who have not made the switch. In the US, 85% of EV owners rate charging coverage as good or very good, up from 72% in 2025. That is the highest satisfaction figure among the surveyed markets.

Only 42% of non-EV owners give charging coverage a positive rating. The 43-point gap suggests that direct experience may make drivers more comfortable with the network than they were beforehand.

And that’s despite the massive infrastructure progress we’ve seen this year. US public charging points grew by more than 14% between 2025 and 2026, while average charger power increased from 65kW to 83kW, a 28% rise.

In terms of costs, well, that’s a different problem. Just 34% of US respondents believe EVs are cheaper to own than gasoline-powered vehicles. Another 29% say costs are about the same, while 28% consider EVs more expensive.

There is a brighter picture among people who already own electric cars: 77% of US EV owners say they are likely to buy another one. The report also pointed out that the end of purchase incentives in late 2025 contributed to dampened EV sales into 2026.

Automakers have two jobs: keep current EV owners happy, and somehow win over the skeptics who still worry about price, charging, and whether an EV fits their daily grind. Sure, faster chargers and more plugs make life easier for EV owners, but that doesn’t mean gas-car drivers are suddenly sold. Carmakers still need to prove EVs make sense for the wallet and won’t mess up anyone’s routine.

Right now, America’s EV market has a first-timer problem. Existing owners are mostly on board for round two, but getting more gas-car drivers to take the plunge is still the real challenge.

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

Models like the Valhalla are helping AM turn things around, though the financial challenges are far from over.

Inside Doug DeMuro's Secret Underground Car Garage

McLaren's Manual V8 McL 6GT Makes Its Public Debut in Las Vegas

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Despite its financial struggles, Aston Martin continues to produce some remarkable cars, including the Valkyrie, which features a naturally aspirated V12 in an era of engine downsizing, and more recently, the open-top Valhalla, capable of matching the coupe’s 217-mph top speed. However, these engineering achievements haven’t translated into significant financial success, as the British automaker continues to struggle six years after Canadian billionaire Lawrence Stroll led a rescue investment in 2020.

According to Bloomberg, citing Aston Martin’s Q3 2026 financial results, the automaker reported a pretax loss of £77 million ($102 million), narrowing from £111.9 million ($148 million) a year earlier. Its net loss also fell from £131.8 million ($175 million) to £78.8 million ($104 million). Despite the improvement, the company’s net debt reached £1.57 billion ($2.1 billion), while cumulative after-tax losses since Stroll’s takeover have reached £2.3 billion ($3.1 billion).

Interestingly, Aston Martin’s wholesale deliveries remained virtually unchanged at 1,431 vehicles in Q3 2026, compared with 1,430 a year earlier. Still, revenue increased 36% to £389 million ($515 million), while gross profit jumped 76%. This improvement reflects a richer sales mix.

The improvements are partly driven by the Valhalla, the brand’s first PHEV supercar, rivaling the likes of the Ferrari 849 Testarossa and Lamborghini Revuelto. The Valhalla was initially capped at 999 examples, although combined coupe and Spider production is now expected to slightly exceed that figure. Such exclusive, high-priced models could help improve profitability, a strategy that has also worked for luxury brands like Rolls-Royce.

The new Valhalla Spider is expected to cost about 20% more than the coupe, which could further help profitability. There’s also the Valen, another limited-series model touted as the world’s most powerful front-engined production car. Arriving in Q2 2027, the Valen comes with a 5.2-liter twin-turbocharged V12 producing 838 horsepower, about 19 hp more than the Ferrari 12Cilindri, though the Ferrari supercar retains a naturally aspirated setup.

It remains to be seen how Aston Martin’s upcoming models and improving financial performance will help the automaker overcome its mounting debt and return to profitability. The company continues to face challenges, including weaker demand in China, U.S. tariffs, and more recently, legal challenges from bondholders such as Arini Capital over its financing arrangements.

Beyond production cars, Stroll has also been investing heavily in Formula 1, where the Aston Martin team, which operates separately from the road-car company, serves as a global marketing platform for the luxury brand. The team has also partnered with Honda as its exclusive power unit supplier since the start of the 2026 season, a collaboration that could eventually lead to a jointly developed road car.

#4420. Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green). Each is priced at $1,399 and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.

So while the underlying bike remains largely unchanged from the bones of the XP 750, the new packages are designed to make the XP4 even more useful straight out of the box.

The District edition is aimed squarely at urban commuters, sporting a stealthy Matte Black finish and an accessory package designed for daily transportation.

That includes two waterproof pannier bags, a redesigned LevelUp rear cargo rack, a heavy-duty bike lock, and an upgraded high-output headlight. There’s also a fast charger, suspension seat post with comfort saddle, and handlebar phone mount.

It’s essentially a ready-made commuter setup, particularly for riders looking to replace some of their car trips with an e-bike.

The Jubilee edition takes a more casual approach, arriving in a distinctive Matte Thistle colorway. Designed for neighborhood cruising, weekend errands, and trips to the local farmers market, it swaps the commuter-focused panniers for a front and rear cargo package and a small roll-top bag.

It also includes the upgraded headlight, lock, fast charger, suspension seat post, comfort saddle, and phone mount.

Finally, the Ridge edition is built for riders who prefer their adventures a bit farther from the pavement.

Finished in Matte Forest green, the Ridge comes with front and rear cargo accessories for carrying outdoor gear, plus a fishing rod holder on the High-Step version. The Step-Thru model instead receives a weather-resistant roll-top bag.

Like the other two editions, the Ridge also includes the upgraded lighting, lock, charger, and comfort accessories.

“We wanted to deliver ready-made, purpose-built setups that empower our community to jump on and ride without having to configure their gear from scratch,” explained Lectric co-founder and CEO Levi Conlow.

Conlow also seems particularly proud of the new finishes, calling them the three best paint jobs Lectric has produced in its seven-year history.

While the new colors and accessory bundles are the main attraction, the bikes retain the same core features that helped make the XP4 such a popular choice.

That includes Lectric’s in-house developed dynamic torque sensor, which measures how hard the rider pedals to deliver a more natural-feeling electric assist experience.

The bikes also feature hydraulic disc brakes, an 8-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain, and a full-color TFT display.

As with the standard XP4, riders get the familiar folding frame design, integrated turn signals and brake lights, and 20-inch puncture-resistant mixed-terrain tires.

All three limited editions are available in both High-Step and Step-Thru frame configurations.

At $1,399, the new models aren’t trying to reinvent the XP4 formula. Instead, they’re offering a more fully equipped version of a bike that has already proven itself with American riders.

And that’s probably a smart move. Lectric has built its reputation on delivering an impressive amount of e-bike for the money, and bundling useful accessories into a relatively affordable package plays right into that strategy.

The limited-edition models are available now, though Lectric says quantities are strictly limited.

For riders who have been considering an XP4 but wanted something a bit more distinctive than the standard colors, these new editions could be a compelling reason to finally pull the trigger.

And for those looking to score an even better deal, Lectric has also officially kicked off its Black Friday sale.

The company is calling it its biggest sale of the year, with some of its lowest prices ever and discounts of up to $800 across its lineup.

So whether you’re eyeing one of the new limited-edition XP4 models or another e-bike in Lectric’s extensive catalog, now could be a particularly good time to buy.

For over 30 years, Ferrari has been letting its customers race its cars in one-make championships. It started in 1993 with the 348, first around Europe, then with a North American series, and later in other parts of the world.

The cars have changed a lot since then. The 348 Challenge became the F355 Challenge, and its successors have become the go-to for the racing series. But in 2003, Ferrari thought it would be a good idea to sell road-going versions of the race cars to even more customers who’d like the experience without having to enter the championship series.

The result was the 360 Challenge Stradale, effectively a road-legal version of the actual race car. At the time, it was matched up against the 911 GT3 RS of the 996.2 generation, and it made for very interesting comparisons. But while Porsche continued building stripped-out, lightweight road-legal racing 911s, Ferrari did not.

But after more than 20 years, Ferrari is bringing back the 296 Challenge Stradale. Like many of 360 Challenge Stradale, it’s taking about four years to get it done, but it’s reportedly coming before the end of the year. That’s according to The Supercar Blog, and that’s not the only bit of information that the publication managed to obtain.

Previously, it was said that the 296 Challenge Stradale would debut sometime in November. Now, a date appears to have been locked in, and it’s slated to premiere during Finali Mondiali at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya. If so, it’s a fitting way to end the 2026 Ferrari Challenge season, which will be held from November 17 to 23. Ferrari will pull the covers off the car on the 21st, and prices are said to start at €320,000 or around $358,000.

The first Challenge Stradale model in over 20 years was first spied back in February. The camouflaged prototype was seen driving around the streets of Maranello, sporting a unique aero package that also includes a whopper of a rear wing among other things.

It’s said that the car won’t have the standard 296’s plug-in hybrid system. If true, that means it’ll be exactly like the 296 Challenge that has been running around the world’s circuits for about three years now. For power, we can expect around 690 hp, which is far less than the hybrid model; the removal of the electrified bits does mean it’s over 300 lbs lighter at the very least. Of course, the Stradale will have some creature comforts, but we’re expecting it to weigh closer to 3,000 lbs. For comparison, the hybrid coupe tips the scales at over 3,500 lbs.

Of course, Ferrari can eke out more horses out of its twin-turbo V6 to make up the difference for losing the electric boost. It’s been rumored that it’ll have about 720 hp, which actually makes it more powerful than the race car. Of course, the race car is a far lighter vehicle, but that’s not to say the Stradale will be a blunt instrument. Mind you, Ferrari may have a couple more track-focused cars coming soon, and 2027 might just be an exciting year for the Prancing Horse.
