After revealing a slew of low-slung SEMA concepts last week, including a rad 300-horsepower Sentra SE-R Spec-V, Nissan is turning its attention to something considerably taller. The automaker is bringing three truck and SUV concepts to the 2026 SEMA Show, showcasing different interpretations of off-road capability and customization. One of them is the Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol, which takes the full-size SUV in a rather unconventional direction.

Inspired by rugged Nissan vehicles that have tackled challenging environments worldwide, including the Patrol, the Jungle Patrol concept is designed around the idea of an expedition-ready machine. It trades much of the Armada’s conventional SUV character for an open-air configuration, specialized off-road hardware, and a safari-inspired cabin. The result is a vehicle that looks more suited to exploring remote trails than navigating the school run.

The most noticeable change is the open-roof configuration, which removes the conventional roof in favor of a tubular steel roll cage. Nissan also fitted custom inward-facing bench seats with harnesses, giving the cabin the appearance of a traditional safari vehicle.

Outside, the Armada gets decked out with jungle-themed graphics, beefy tubular steel bumpers, and fender flares that mean business. NISMO Off Road throws in roof-mounted six-inch lights and rock sliders, so you can light up the trail and bash rocks without breaking a sweat.

The concept also gets a substantial suspension upgrade. Its widened track incorporates custom CJD long-travel racing suspension, featuring adjustable high-performance coilovers with remote reservoirs. This setup is paired with prototype NISMO 18-inch AXIS beadlock wheels wrapped in 37×12.50R18 Yokohama Geolandar G003 M/T tires.

Under the hood, the Armada retains its direct-injected 3.5-liter VR35 V6 engine. The standard powerplant produces 425 horsepower and 516 lb-ft of torque. Nissan adds a prototype NISMO cat-back exhaust system, while Mobil 1 Extended Performance Oil is also included in the build.

The Armada Jungle Patrol is only one of three concepts Nissan prepared for this year’s SEMA Show. Nissan says these concepts are intended to inspire owners to personalize their vehicles while allowing its designers and engineers to gather feedback on potential future accessories and product directions.

The company also pointed toward its upcoming all-new Xterra, suggesting that more capable trucks and SUVs remain part of its future plans. However, none of the three SEMA builds will become production models in their current form – though Nissan says some accessories featured on the concepts may eventually be available through dealerships.

The 2026 SEMA Show runs from November 3 to 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center in Las Vegas, Nevada. Visitors can find Nissan’s concepts at booth No. 21521 in Central Hall.

#4358. Eternal Anima Hands-On Preview – Strive How I Want To

Eternal Anima is the time-twisting RPG revealed during the big September Nintendo Direct that looked like a Square Enix HD-2D game but isn’t. It is also the game with the “Never Strive For A Better Tomorrow” splash screen. After playing the game for roughly an hour within developer Marvelous Inc.’s Tokyo office, I eschew that line – I will, in fact, strive for a better tomorrow, if only so I can play more Eternal Anima one day.

The world has essentially come to its final act in Eternal Anima. Urvis Ael is the last remaining bastion of civilization in a flooded world. That said, living in Urvis Ael isn’t all that bad; just don’t strive for a better tomorrow or really any kind of change. Protagonist Wade breaks those rules and sets out on an adventure, feeling deep down that a better life is possible.

Wade is bestowed with the power of Psychometry, which lets him look into the past, view memories, and inherit abilities and classes for use in combat. My hands-on time with Eternal Anima is mostly focused on combat, and for good reason: it rules. It is turn-based combat, but with a time-turning twist. Wade also has the power of Future Sight, which means he already knows exactly what every enemy will do each turn, reflected in the UI. Every ability has an action speed shown on the timeline at the bottom of the screen. You can always see an enemy’s upcoming action, who they will target, and even the outcome.

Combat in Eternal Anima is less about hitting enemies harder and more about hitting them smarter. When you attack an enemy's weaknesses with Wade or other party members, you knock them back on the battle timeline, pushing their predecided actions back in the move queue. Your goal is to push them back enough that you kill them before they can attack, or, for bigger enemies, knock them off the timeline in what’s known as a Break. This cancels their action, opening up your party for another round of attacks.

The battle system doesn’t feel as active as a standard turn-based RPG; instead, it makes you feel more like a god playing with action figures. You decide what happens, then sit back and watch it all unfold.

Everything is depicted in a beautiful, bokeh-enhanced art style that’s unique to Eternal Anima, despite the initial HD-2D impression. I love how the world and enemies look, which makes it even more disappointing that the characters are rendered as chibi. It doesn’t gel with the game’s painterly visuals and clashes with its heavier thematic tones.

As I explore Eternal Anima’s miniature settings, which resemble closed-off dioramas placed carefully on a larger world map, I take part in fishing minigames, collect items, defeat enemies, and encounter NPCs from the past, like Fletcher. After I interact with a glowing sword on the ground, an animated flashback plays, detailing Fletcher’s story and ending with a notification that I received a bow from his past.

As I continue through this world, some two centuries before my time, I encounter a man from this period who’s trying to save his forest hometown from flooding. Of course, I already know this will happen in my timeline because the entire world is flooded, but Wade suspects that if he can convince this person of the looming threat, he can change the present by altering the past. My demo ends shortly after, but now, a month removed from the preview, I’m still thinking about Eternal Anima, specifically its combat.

A lot of turn-based combat makes you feel powerful. But Eternal Anima’s makes you feel like a genius, and that’s smart and novel. I’m left striving for March now.

#4357. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

The Frontier’s 3.8-liter V-6 is still present under the hood of the Ronin, but Nissan also made a host of notable changes. For starters, the Ronin features forced induction in the form of the R35 Nissan GT-R’s twin-turbo setup, which is mounted in the rear.

#4353. Nissan Turns the Armada into the Safari-Ready Jungle Patrol Concept

The Armada Jungle Patrol loses its roof, rides on a custom long-travel suspension, and wears tubular bumpers and lots of auxiliary lighting.

Each year, the SEMA show in Las Vegas allows automakers to let their creativity shine through custom concepts based on production vehicles. In 2025, Nissan turned its full-size Armada SUV into the desert-ready Dune Patrol, adding a long-travel suspension, unique bumpers, and a durable roof rack. Now, for 2026, Nissan has modified the Armada once again, this time transforming it into the Jungle Patrol, ripping off the roof to make the SUV into the ideal safari companion.

The Armada Jungle Patrol’s biggest change is, obviously, the lack of a roof, with the solid shelter replaced by a tubular roll cage, providing a better view of the natural world you’re exploring. Just be ready to speed away if a lion gets a little too curious about the tasty treats sitting inside. The rear section has been fitted with inward-facing bench seats, a common setup in safari vehicles.

See all results for new 2026 Nissan Armada for sale near 39759

Nissan also upgraded the Armada to tackle more serious terrain. The Jungle Patrol rides on prototype 18-inch NISMO wheels wrapped in 37-inch Yokohama Geolandar G003 M/T tires, which are suspended on a custom long-travel setup from CJD Racing. The setup utilizes high-performance adjustable coil-overs with remote reservoirs and bypass, and the Jungle Patrol has a wider track than the regular Armada.

The Jungle Patrol is also equipped with custom steel bumpers and fender flares, and there are NISMO off-road lights mounted on the bumper and roof to illuminate the jungle at night. Nissan caps off the look with a unique livery, which reads “Jungle Patrol” in a scrawled font and features what look like the claw marks of some intimidating jungle beast down the rear doors.

As with the Desert Patrol last year, Nissan has left the standard 425-hp twin-turbo 3.5-liter V-6 engine untouched but added a custom NISMO cat-back exhaust. While the Armada Jungle Patrol is a fun experiment, we assume it will never enter production given its extreme mission, but some features, like the prototype wheels and custom bumpers, could one day be offered as official NISMO aftermarket parts.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.

#4351. Our Long-Term 2026 Honda Passport Is Still a Hot Commodity

With its plush interior and a commodious cargo hold, our boxy Honda has become the car-board-lottery jackpot for those planning a road trip.

“I’ve finally won!” exclaims technical editor Austin Irwin in response to snagging our long-term 2026 Honda Passport TrailSport for the weekend. Typically, it’s sports cars, rolling palaces, or vehicles with a manual transmission that elicit that type of reaction during our weekly sign-out process, not mid-size two-row SUVs. But the Passport really does have that effect on folks around here.

While it’s nowhere near the most engaging vehicle at our office at any given time, our sunburnt Honda’s allure comes from its ability to effortlessly eat both cargo and miles in large sums. Depending on your weekend plans, that can be far more valuable than the Hattori Hanzō–sharp steering precision of a 911 or the rewarding snick of a Miata’s six-speed shifter.

In the 10,000 miles since we last checked in, a handful of editors have taken full advantage of the Passport’s strengths. In just a few short months, it checked Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Ohio off its regional-visitation checklist, with one sentiment echoed by the three staffers upon returning from their respective excursions: The Passport is a damn good road tripper.

See all results for new 2026 Honda Passport for sale near 33486

“Taking the Passport on a trip through Ohio to Hocking Hills was very enjoyable,” said online production assistant Sarah Taylor, who specifically called out its smooth ride and competent handling on winding mountain roads. Senior social media editor Carter Fry also joined in on praising the Honda’s on-road demeanor, noting that the SUV “is so well balanced considering its size and all-terrain tires.” A plush ride and confidence-inspiring handling are important traits on long-distance trips, but the Passport’s comfortable and expansive interior is what really cements it as our resident road-trip hero.

“Cavernous,” “spacious,” and “generous” have all appeared in the Passport’s in-car logbook to describe its cargo accommodations, and it is indeed very roomy back there by mid-size-SUV standards. In our testing, we managed to stuff under its liftgate 16 carry-on suitcases with the rearmost seats in their upright position and 38 carry-ons with the rear bench folded down. That’s 13 and nine more than will fit in a Toyota 4Runner, respectively. Managing news editor Eric Stafford did his best to stretch the Passport’s people and stuff-hauling capabilities to their limit on a ski trip to northern Wisconsin and reported that there was more than enough room to comfortably accommodate three guys and all their gear. So far, no one has been able to find anything that doesn’t fit in the Passport's cargo hold, but we’ll keep brainstorming.

As far as grievances are concerned, there haven’t been many. Several editors have reported software issues related to phone pairing, Google Maps connectivity, and Apple CarPlay glitches. On one occasion, the infotainment screen went blank but continued to play music from the grave. On another, the GPS display within the digital gauge cluster got confused and gave up despite that Android Auto was running with no connectivity issues. Both of those incidents were resolved with a simple restart. Aside from that, there’s an ambiguous logbook comment likening the Passport’s interior to “something you’d order out of an L.L. Bean catalog,” but it's unclear whether that was meant as a compliment or a dig. Depends on how much you like cable-knit sweaters, we suppose.

See all results for new 2026 Honda Passport for sale near 33486

There isn’t much to report from a service or repair standpoint, either. Since we took in the Passport for its 10,000-mile oil service, which was covered under Honda’s one-year, 12,000-mile complimentary maintenance coverage, the sole out-of-pocket expense we’ve incurred was for the Passport’s 20,000-mile service, which included an oil and filter change, a tire rotation, and an inspection, for a total of $184. The only change to the TrailSport’s hardware was a swap back to its original 275/60R-18 General Grabber A/T Sport tires after the shedding of its Continental VikingContact 8 winters, but we handled that ourselves.

While it’s uncommon for a family SUV to be a first-round pick in an office full of performance-pilled enthusiasts, it’s clear why our long-term Passport is so highly coveted. With its coddling seats, plush but poised ride quality, and seemingly boundless cargo hold, the Passport is a hard act to beat when you’re staring down a thousand-mile road trip. As long as C/D staffers remain adventurous, we’re sure that the Passport’s key fob will continue to be fought over in the 20,000 miles to come.

The first few months of a new job can be stressful, especially when you have more than 20 professional scrutinizers judging you at all times, constantly scheming new ways to push you until your wheels fall off. Some might call that a hostile work environment, but that’s daily life for the vehicles in the Car and Driver long-term test fleet. While some of our long-termers are progressively eased into their 40,000 miles of hard labor, our Honda Passport TrailSport Elite was afforded no such luxury. Soon after it got acquainted with its new handlers, we threw it headfirst into the ultimate utility litmus test as a support vehicle for our most recent Lightning Lap event.

For those unfamiliar with our annual gantlet of speed, here are the CliffsNotes: We round up the newest street-legal performance cars and set course for Virginia International Raceway in Alton, Virginia. Once there, our editors attack the 4.1-mile Grand Course configuration with as much aplomb as they dare, reporting back with lap times and harrowing tales of grit and grandeur from behind the wheel. It is quite the production, and with 16 vehicles in need of attention at this year's event, a capable gear hauler was as important as ever.

We decided that a 12-foot U-Haul box trailer would best suit our needs, so we rented one and loaded it with items crucial for the operation, including jacks, jack stands, scales, test equipment, tires, a grill, and a hot-dog rotisserie. After filling the trailer well short of the Passport's 5000-pound maximum towing capacity, we backed our rig up to its new companion for the 600-plus-mile journey to the Virginia–North Carolina border. Mating the two was easy with the TrailSport Elite's multiview backup camera. Our only gripe was the position of our Passport's hitch receiver, which was a little low for our use case, but we made it work. With the supplies loaded and a full tank of gas, we hit the road.

Road warrior Christi VanSyckle was tasked with piloting our traffic-cone-colored Honda across multiple state lines and the Appalachian Mountains. She arrived at the track with a positive report card for the Passport, saying that “stability was confident at highway speeds through the mountains.” She added that the cabin was surprisingly quiet and the seats provided enough support that she never felt the need to stop and stretch. Gold stars for comfort and capability. Nothing changed on the return trip, so we'd say that the Passport aced its doozy of an initiation test.

Back home, the Passport was finally given the chance to settle into a more mundane daily rhythm. It continued to draw praise as more editors had the chance to slide behind the wheel. In the logbook comments that trickled in, one comparison continued to pop up: "It used to be the Accord sedan, but the V-6 family Honda is now an SUV. I'm surprisingly okay with it," said editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga. That thought was echoed by staff photographer Michael Simari, who mused, "The Passport's Accord-like agreeableness continues to grow on me."

Being likened to the 40-time 10Best-winning Honda Accord is quite the compliment, and the comparison makes a lot of sense considering the Passport shares the Accord's practical, ergonomically satisfying, and well-rounded demeanor. Its softly sprung ride makes long-distance travel comfortable and effortless, and its voluminous rear cabin grants back-seat passengers an especially generous amount of stretch-out space. Up front, the 12.3-inch touchscreen is quick to respond to inputs, and the physical steering-wheel buttons and climate-control toggles are positioned just right. Some drivers have experienced Apple CarPlay connectivity issues, but that is likely due in part to the dozens of phones constantly cycling through our car's system.

While our time with the Passport has been mostly smiles so far, a couple of sore spots have surfaced. The 3.5-liter V-6 under the hood has received mixed reviews, with the main pain point being its lack of low-rpm grunt. Its full 262 pound-feet of peak torque doesn't arrive until 5000 rpm, which, combined with our test vehicle's 4702 pounds, leads to a notable delay in gumption after kicking the go pedal. One comment also mentioned the 10-speed automatic's indifferent attitude toward downshifting, which contributes to the malaise, especially during city driving and highway merging. These gripes have led some staffers to contemplate what the Passport would be like with an alternative powerplant, with video deputy editor Carlos Lago positing that "a hybrid system would make this feel much punchier, à la Grand Highlander Hybrid."

A hybrid powertrain would also work wonders for the Passport's fuel efficiency, which has nonetheless been reasonable thus far. After more than 10,000 miles, we're averaging 19 mpg, which is 1 mpg less than the TrailSport's EPA combined rating yet a decent figure considering it includes the round trip to VIR with a trailer in tow.

A recent swap to Continental VikingContact 8 winter tires, which set us back a little under $930 with installation, also is likely impacting our fuel economy, but with southeastern Michigan doing its best snow-globe impression over the past few months, it's been a welcome switch. The slightly narrower winter rubber—sized 265/60R-18 versus the OE-spec 275/60R-18s—has made drudging through the polar-apocalyptic wasteland easy, providing nearly undefeatable grip on glassy interstates and unplowed side roads. Road warrior Jacob Kurowicki pointed out that the new tires are a double-edged sword, saying, "This thing is too damn capable in the snow on these winter tires. Being a hooligan requires some commitment." While ride quality hasn’t been impacted to any noticeable degree, cabin noise levels certainly have. Managing testing editor Dave Beard isn't a fan of the racket, proclaiming, "These tires are already getting annoying. How soon can we install some BFGoodrich KO3s?"

So far, the Passport has made two trips to the dealer. The first was at around 6200 miles, when a TD02 code was triggered for a supposed over-the-air software update failure. Resetting the system resulted in a fresh S404 (update unavailable) code, for which the dealer had no solution. We're hoping a future software update will resolve the matter. The second stop was for an oil change, tire rotation, and rear differential fluid change at roughly 10,200 miles. Both services were free under Honda's one-year or 12,000-mile complimentary maintenance coverage, and we haven't encountered any other issues that would force us to fork over some dough.

Despite the abhorrent weather, our time with the Passport has been mostly sunny. Even faced with a particularly difficult challenge right out of the gate, our long-termer has proved its worth as a formidable hauler, a practical errand-runner, and a comfortable road-trip companion.

Since the Honda Passport was revived for the 2019 model year, it has racked up some significant Car and Driver accolades. Upon its return to the market, the Passport promptly conquered its contemporaries in a five-car two-row mid-size-SUV comparison test. After its strong showing, we invited a 2019 Passport EX-L to live with us for a while, where it proved to be a comfortable, practical, and (mostly) unproblematic companion for 40,000 miles. The Passport has also earned a spot on our Editors' Choice list every year since its revival, and now it has joined the ranks among the industry's best as a 2026 10Best laureate.

While the outgoing generation was certainly deserving of the praise it received, one thing was desperately missing from its arsenal: allure. The Passport had utility mastered, but its anonymous styling and drab interior made it as appetizing as boiled chicken. Honda has addressed that point with the new 2026 Passport, which now looks much more appealing with its brawny, cubist sheetmetal and enhanced capabilities. With it now more flavorful, we're going in for a second serving, inviting the Passport back for another 40,000-mile stress test.

When it came time to spec our new long-termer, we had an important decision to make. While every 2026 Passport comes with all-wheel drive, a 3.5-liter V-6, and a 10-speed automatic transmission, there's a sizable difference between the base RTL and the off-road-focused TrailSport. Plenty of C/D staffers aren't afraid to get dirty, so we decided to pull the trigger on a TrailSport Elite to ensure that no mud pit would go uncrossed.

While the Passport is still not quite as capable as some of the body-on-frame options in the segment, such as the Toyota 4Runner or the Ford Bronco, it's clear that tough-terrain capability was a top priority for the newest Passport. As with all other TrailSport models, our TrailSport Elite comes with plenty of gear to aid in our off-pavement antics, including skid plates that provide genuine underbody protection, an off-road-oriented suspension tune, a torque-vectoring rear axle within the all-wheel-drive system, easy-access recovery points that are rated for twice the Passport's weight, and 18-inch wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires. An integrated trailer hitch rated for 5000 pounds of towing capacity comes standard, as do amber daytime running lights, which are less about function but really add some unique character to the Passport's facia.

While we left the boxes on our long-termer's rather short options list largely unchecked (other than the one for Sunset Orange paint at $455), the TrailSport Elite is jam-packed with its fair share of luxuries as a premium trim in the Passport model hierarchy. Standard features include heated and ventilated leather front seats, a panoramic moonroof, heated side mirrors, a Bose audio system, a power liftgate, puddle lights, a heated leather 60/40-split rear bench seat, and a 12.3-inch infotainment touchscreen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Our final tally: $54,355.

Regardless of trim, the Passport is powered by a 285-hp 3.5-liter V-6 mated to a 10-speed automatic transmission. There is no other engine available. While the 2026 Passport's double-overhead-cam V-6 makes five more horsepower than the outgoing generation's 280-hp SOHC 3.5-liter V-6, the new model's additional weight obviates any gains made by the updated powertrain from an acceleration standpoint. The verdict on the Passport's gumption is split, with some noting that it feels quick enough and others musing if it feels underpowered.

Regardless of our subjective opinions, numbers don't lie, and our TrailSport Elite is much slower than the previous-generation Passport. At the test track, our new TrailSport Elite took 7.1 seconds to reach 60 mph—1.2 seconds slower than a 2024 Passport TrailSport that we tested. While a 7.1-second 60-mph time is far from blistering, it's still quicker than a nonhybrid Toyota 4Runner or a nonturbo Subaru Outback.

Lateral grip is one area where the new Passport made significant gains on its predecessor, with our TrailSport Elite circling the skidpad at a respectable 0.84 g compared with 0.74 g for the previous version. Its larger 275/60R-18 General Grabber A/T Sport tires (compared with 245/60R-18 Grabbers on the 2024 TrailSport), in addition to its suspension upgrades and a significantly stiffer chassis, can be mostly credited for the significant increase in grip between generations. Tipping the scales at 4702 pounds, our 2026 rig marginally improved upon its 4237-pound predecessor's braking performance, requiring 177 feet to come to a stop from 70 mph; the 2024 model took 181 feet to stop from the same speed.

The Passport didn't pull off any groundbreaking feats at the track, but its on-road comportment, well-fitted interior, and commodious cargo space have made it a growing favorite among the staff. The TrailSport Elite's muscular new look seems to be a hit—a stark contrast to the last generation, which had as much visual intrigue as a bowl of nonfat Greek yogurt. Several editors have also complimented its comfortable ride and agreeable, if somewhat dull, on-road dynamics. By far the most common praises have been about the Passport's roomy interior and luggage-eating cargo hold, spaces which feel almost geometry-defying within a mid-size-SUV envelope.

After a few months with the Passport, the collective outlook for our sun-kissed Honda is optimistic. As we venture deeper into what is turning out to be a frigid Michigan winter, our Passport will be subjected to grueling Midwest snowstorms, icy roads, and any wintertime shenanigans our editors can dream up. We'll check in again at the 10,000-mile mark to let you know what those shenanigans entail as the miles add up.

#4350. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 16, 2026

Welcome to spooky month where lawns suddenly grow giant skeletons, it's cold enough for a hoodie, the remakes of Resident Evil 2, 3, and 4 released on Switch 2, and we're all prepping to hunker down for Winter. And Grand Theft Auto VI.

We're still in the thick of new release season which, fun fact, used to just be the month of November. But now it starts in August and ends in March, give or take a few weeks.

Before we get to our regularly scheduled weekend recommendations, though, here are some of the biggest Game Informer stories of the week.

It has been a long wait for a brand new Castlevania game, and frankly, I think Belmont's Curse has been worth the time spent in the queue. Charles Harte agrees, as he wrote in his review, "Belmont's Curse is a strong reminder of why the Castlevania series is so influential, with a rich world, tense combat, and a map chock-full of secrets. While this latest entry certainly pays homage to the Castlevanias of yore, it also breathes fresh life into the franchise, making me excited for its future. Castlevania is back, and between Rose Belmont and Evil Empire, it's in great hands."

The game comes from the team behind Dead Cells, a game heavily influenced by Castlevania to begin with, and the result shows how great a fit the team and franchise is. Controlling Rose Belmont feels great, the world is big and fun to explore without being overbearing, and beating each boss is a rewarding challenge. I often feel one mark of a good game for me is if it keeps me up past my bedtime, and Belmont's Curse is, unfortunately, doing a great job of making me feel tired all day. But that's a good thing.

The short pitch for Silver Pines is that it is a Metroid-inspired game crossed with a Silent Hill game. That's a good hook on its own, but what makes it stand out (at least in the limited time I have so far spent with it), is its animation. I don't know that it was actually rotoscoped (think the original 1989 Prince of Persia), but it feels like it was, which makes it look great and lends it an intentional level of uncanny valley that aids the creepy atmosphere. Throw in a dash of Twin Peaks energy, and you end up with something that feels unique against a sea of comparable (but often well-designed) Metroid-inspired games.

Just Dance is an frequent tradition in my household. We don't play it every year, but I was eager to check out Decades of Hits because of its included soundtrack. Just Dance generally leans on contemporary music and as a dad facing down his forties (who is still very cool, right? Right?!) I appreciate the chance to learn about recent pop hits and make a fool of myself in front of my family, but I like how musically diverse this entry is.

You have Sabrina Carpenter, Chappell Roan, and Olivia Rodrigo songs (which I adore), but you also get ABBA, Spice Girls, No Doubt, Daft Punk, Britney Spears, Sum 41, TLC, Gorillaz, Run DMC, Billy Joel, and Elton John among many others.

Also, in recent years, Just Dance has started its own tradition of including at least one shockingly impressive stop-motion animated sequence. I am not sure what executive at Ubisoft is accidentally approving the budget for the continued creation of these types of videos, but I hope they never notice because they're great.

You really can’t go wrong with any Jackbox game. Sure, there are some occasional duds in the packages, but there are always at least one or two super fun games that are always worth returning to. 12 is out this week and includes a game about sorting trivia questions into the right categories at high speed, one where you try to make the most ridiculous greeting card, a game encouraging silly debates, one that identifies connections among everyone playing, and finally Hyperface, where you manipulate selfies.

After an earlier release on VR platforms, the rhythm game Maestro recently made its way onto Switch and Switch 2, including a physical game cartridge launch. If you've always secretly loved the idea of stepping up onto the podium for a try at the conductor's gig, it's one worth tracking down. The game includes a number of classical hits from the likes of Beethoven, Vivaldi, and Tchaikovsky, but there's also the chance to play more contemporary tracks like those you'd hear in Star Wars or Game of Thrones. With Joy-Cons in hand, you'll keep the tempo, cue in musicians, adjust dynamics, and more. The accompanying visuals and "storytelling" aren't going to blow your mind, but the included music is hard to beat, and with occasional exceptions where the game misread my motions, I found the motion-tracking mostly up to the task of nailing the fantasy.

If you spent hours playing the early Toy Story games, then the retro compilation masters at Digital Eclipse have something for you in the form of Toy Story: Retro Roundup. On top of Toy Story, Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue, Toy Story 2, Buzz Lightyear of Star Command, and Toy Story Racer (including multiple versions of many of these), you can also get your hands on the 1998 A Bug's Life game. It may not have the breadth of extra content of something like Digital Eclipse's Atari 50 or Tetris Forever, but it's a fun stroll down memory lane with some behind-the-scenes interviews and materials. Alongside this retro collection, there's also the separate Toy Story 3 Complete Edition, also released by Digital Eclipse this week.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] – yes, that’s really what it’s called – is out on Nintendo Switch 2, and after spending some time with it, man, it feels right at home on the console. This collection includes Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 +2.5 ReMix (which itself includes a bunch of Kingdom Hearts games, including 1 and 2), Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, and Kingdom Hearts III + Re Mind DLC. Basically, it has everything you need to catch up on the Kingdom Hearts saga before Kingdom Hearts IV launches next year.

As for actually playing these games, they feel amazing on Switch 2, courtesy of HD resolutions, on handheld and docked, and 60 FPS gameplay. I don’t know why exactly, but playing the Kingdom Hearts series on Switch 2 just feels right. It probably has something to do with just how many of these games were Nintendo console originals. Nonetheless, if you’re new to Kingdom Hearts or looking for a new place to tear up while "Dearly Beloved" plays, this Switch 2 collection will satisfy your needs.

This new standalone version of Forest Shuffle does more than transplant the theming into the Smoky Mountains of North America. It has also allowed its creators to refine balance, add new elements (like an intriguing new water/river terrain), create a more vibrant and visually beautiful presentation, and overall, up the value and playability of the game across the board. In short, it's what I think is the best version of an already very good game.

For newcomers, the Forest Shuffle formula is a card game that involves a mix of card hand management and tableau-building, as you slowly play out a forest scene onto the table, filled with unique trees, animals, and plants, and gathering points for the types and variety of things living in your woods. It's an approachable and visually enchanting game that still offers plenty of strategic depth as you plan out the shape and potential of your nature scene, all while planning against the impending arrival of winter.

#4349. Tested: Best Home EV Chargers for 2026

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Make the most of EV ownership with high-voltage home charging equipment. We tested some of the top home EV chargers on the market to find the best.

This article was updated in November 2026. We plan to update this test regularly as we evaluate additional units.

Okay, so you bought an electric vehicle. Now what? There are a number of ways in which EV ownership will be different from having a vehicle with an internal-combustion engine, but a big one you need to figure out immediately is charging. Trust us, you'll want to be charging at home as much as possible. What's the best EV charger for your home?

Owning a home EV charger has two significant benefits: Charging can be accomplished when the vehicle is otherwise parked, and home charging is substantially cheaper (roughly one-third the cost) than DC fast-charging. On average, EV charging equipment will have an up-front cost of between $400 and $700. But, depending on what equipment came with your EV, you might not need to buy a home unit at all, and could instead make do with the included portable-charging setup.

See all results for used cars for sale near 90011

For this test, I installed a dedicated 240-volt outlet in my garage—just as a new EV owner would need to. I then tested these chargers with Car and Driver's long-term Tesla Model 3, Rivian R1T, BMW i4, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Kia EV9, and Lucid Air Pure—among various other test vehicles—taking notes on each charger's performance in typical daily use. Testing each unit takes months, thanks to the multitude of hours required to charge cars and gather data. We plan on updating this article with new products and testing data twice a year.

see all the best deals on ev chargers at amazon

You may have heard grumbling from EV owners who have had to make an expensive upgrade to their electrical service in order to charge their vehicles. That's what's so great about the Emporia Pro: It comes with the company's Vue 3 energy monitor that installs into your house's electrical panel, allowing the system to adjust the EV-charging output in real time to make sure it doesn't exceed what your house can handle. No panel upgrade needed, but that does make the install more complicated than other chargers that don't have this functionality.

This new Emporia Pro is also much slimmer with a far thinner cable that's easier to wrangle than the company's previous Level 2 home charger, now called the Classic and sold alongside the Pro.

In fact, if you're trying to pinch pennies, you can buy the Vue 3 home energy monitor ($100 at Amazon) and older Classic Level 2 charger separately ($529 combined) and get the same load-balancing capability.

See all results for used cars for sale near 90011

We also found this latest setup from Emporia reacts to charging electrical loads much quicker than before. Either Emporia unit pairs with the same powerful app that also houses info about the plethora of other energy-monitoring devices and smart plugs the company sells (for example, you can monitor each individual circuit breaker in your entire home). It's a powerful and capable app, but if you're only using it for EV charging, it can seem unnecessarily complex.

Emporia offers J1772 or NACS plug types, in hardwire or plug configuration, all for the same price. If you don't need the load-balancing feature, go with the less expensive Emporia Classic below.

Emporia offers a vast library of electricity-monitoring devices, from typical smart outlets to a system that tracks every circuit in your home's fuse panel. This entire electricity-tracking universe is integrated into Emporia's app, including the ability to link your EV to the app through the Smartcar API. But if you're just using the EV-charging equipment, navigating around all of these unused areas makes the app seem overly complex.

Otherwise, this is an impressive Wi-Fi–connected entry at a price hundreds of dollars less than other top chargers. The 11.5-kW-output capability is at the high end, and, short of a couple of features such as using a specific vehicle to estimate the miles or battery percentage gained, the Emporia has just about everything, including detailed electricity pricing using your actual utility plan like the ChargePoint.

The Emporia is available with either a J1772 plug or a NACS/J3400 connector, and comes in either plug-in or hardwire configuration, all for the same price.

This new entry from Michigan-based automotive supplier Danlaw, Inc. is appropriately named, as it's significantly more intelligent than the typical Wi-Fi–connected smart charger. The additional functionality includes tracking energy consumption of your vehicle on each drive, which it uses to arrive at real-world range estimates, and sends notifications when you should plug in based on your driving behavior and how many miles it predicts you'll drive the next day.

The additional smarts are enabled by a dongle that plugs into your vehicle's OBD-II port under the dash, which is also used to communicate with your charging unit to initiate charging while preventing anyone without a registered dongle from doing so. (Note: The driving data is synched when the vehicle is close to the charging unit; it isn't broadcasting the vehicle's drive cycles or location in real time.) For many EVs or PHEVs, its self-reported battery health rating (out of 100 percent) is also displayed in the app. The CleverCharge also comes with other data that's often part of having a dongle plugged in; one time I got an alert with the three error codes that caused a vehicle's check-engine light to illuminate. It also sent me a push notification during a storm that my household voltage was low before a subsequent power outage.

The CleverCharge excels at having multiple charging units and vehicles linked to a single account. We also found it easy to use, and the 25-foot cord is thinner than most, allowing it to easily snake under a closed garage door to charge a vehicle in the driveway. The only major issue is that with vehicles lacking an OBD-II port or communication protocol, such as Tesla, Rivian, and Lucid vehicles, none of the additional features will work.

Despite all the extra smarts, the CleverCharge is priced way down at the low end of the market and, like most of the others, comes in either plug-in or hardwired formats with J1772 or NACS connector.

Lectron's long been on our radar as an affordable maker of EV charging equipment and adapters. In fact, it's one of the go-to suppliers of NACS to SAE adapters for automakers. For this test, we tried out the company's entry-level charging equipment, which looks like a portable unit that might come with the purchase of an EV. But, importantly, the Lectron unit has Wi-Fi connectivity with the capability to control charge times and settings, plus monitor energy use via an app. (There's also a slightly cheaper version of this unit that does without the connectivity.)

It comes with a wall mount to make the installation more permanent, but you'll need to hang your own hook as a place to hang the cord. The app isn't as sophisticated as some from the more expensive chargers, and we don't like that you can't look back at specific charges that are more than a month old (although you can see the overall usage for past months). But there's no need to spend more than this to get a perfectly capable home-charging setup.

ChargePoint is one of the largest providers of public charging, with tens of thousands of units nationwide. Its Home Flex unit tested here integrates into the same app used to connect to the company's public units. You can add your vehicle in the app, which tailors the percentage of the battery replenished and number of EPA miles added to your specific vehicle.

We found the app to be very user-friendly, with the best displays for charge-rate graphs, and it also shows the total charge time and total energy output during each charge. Furthermore, it offers the ability to schedule charging times to take advantage of variable-cost electricity during off-peak hours (most EVs also allow this to be configured in their settings menu).

The ChargePoint app has the most nuanced cost tracking, allowing us to select from among dozens of possible rate plans from our local utility to pinpoint the actual cost of charging down to the penny, even when on a variable rate.

We also appreciate the simplicity of the built-in notch for wrapping the cord around at the top of the unit and that the plug latches onto its dock in the center; many other units require mounting a second cord-management device.

The Universal Wall Connector is Tesla's latest home-charging offering, which has a built-in adapter to switch seamlessly between J1772 and NACS plug types. The unit itself is significantly thicker than the standard Wall Connector with the Tesla plug, but there's a reason for that: the adapter. At first, it appears to be a simple contraption that slides onto the end of a typical Tesla connector, but it's actually electronically locked into place so the adapter can't go missing. Nifty.

Power output remains the same from the standard Wall Connector, which peaks at 11.5 kilowatts, is available only in a hardwire configuration, and has the ability to power share with other Wall Connectors.

In other big news, the unit integrates into the Tesla mobile app to allow monitoring of energy use, which is mandatory if you want to track efficiency like we do with all of our test cars. Once the charging unit is installed, it must be commissioned via a separate Tesla One app, but thankfully, any DIYer can create an account to set up the maximum output for the circuit the unit is connected to, and users can also specify certain Teslas to allow to charge at the unit while blocking others. Unfortunately, that functionality doesn't carry over to non-Tesla vehicles.

The slimness of the Wall Connector's 24-foot-long cable continues to impress us as it matches the output capacity of units with thicker cables. This makes the cord easier to maneuver and leaves a smaller gap when the garage door is closed on it when charging a vehicle in the driveway.

Pricewise, the Universal is at the higher end, but for a mixed-EV household or to future-proof your home-charging setup, this is a great solution.

Going from a single EV in the household to two or more requires a rethink on your charging setup. Grizzl-E offers this Duo unit as an easy solution. It plugs into a single outlet—there are variants for NEMA 6-50 or 14-50 plug types—and has two 24-foot cables with two J1772 connectors to charge two vehicles simultaneously. With one EV plugged in, that side gets all the available juice, up to the unit's or the car's maximum. If you then plug in a second EV, the output immediately splits to half for each cable.

As with other single-plug Grizzl-E home chargers, the enclosure is made of beefy aluminum, and its thick cables resist winding around the included wall mounts more than most. However, this is the least expensive dual-plug charging unit we could find. Other two-vehicle options involve buying two separate charging units wired to two dedicated circuits—which would be far more expensive—or setting up some kind of power-sharing arrangement, where the two units share the output of a single circuit (both the Tesla and Emporia units support this). Another way to do this is to use the Lectron Socket Splitter (see review below).

What the Grizzl-E Duo doesn't offer is a Wi-Fi–connected version to allow users to track their electrical use and cost in a detailed manner or schedule charging via an app. But for a seamless way to charge two EVs simultaneously, the Duo gets the job done.

While technically not EV-charging equipment like the others, this Lectron Socket Splitter is another option for charging two EVs from a single circuit. Think of it sort of like a power strip for 240-volt outlets, where it plugs into your high-voltage outlet and then two individual EV chargers (or household appliances or other equipment) plug into it. The unit prioritizes the left outlet, but once that side stops charging, the unit will start charging the vehicle connected to the other side.

It doesn't ever split the power 50-50 like the Grizzl-E Duo unit does. It works well enough, as long as you make sure there's sufficient time to charge both vehicles—because if the left side never stops charging, the unit will never switch over to the other side. Also, after only a handful of uses, our left outlet started wobbling in place after a trim piece broke inside the unit, although it was still fully functional.

Eviqo is regularly a top seller among EV charging equipment on Amazon, so we figured it was time to check it out. It checks all the usual boxes: 25-foot cord, programmable charge times, and energy tracking. The one exceptional characteristic is that the NEMA 14-50 plug is on a long cable, leaving lots of flexibility with where the unit can be mounted and still reach the outlet. It's also priced at the low end of the market, which no doubt helps its popularity.

But the app isn't nearly as easy to use as the best, for example it's not simple to set up overnight charging to take advantage of lower electricity rates. You have to program two rules: from, say, 7 pm to 11:59 pm, and then a second one to start at 12:00 am. Also, a slider bar to adjust the current output lives prominently on the main screen where you can accidentally bump it, and that's a setting that's rarely used. And you can't go back and look at individual charges, only one-week, one-month, or three-month totals.

Our unit arrived missing the mounting bracket for the wall-mount hook for the charging handle and cable. This seemed like a simple enough oversight, but it took a lot of back-and-forth emails with the customer service team, who would sometimes go five days between responses, to get it resolved. After they agreed to send a replacement, it took another two weeks to get a tracking number. It finally arrived just over six weeks after my initial email to customer service.

When putting together this story, I went down the same path a new EV owner would, starting with installing a dedicated 240-volt outlet in my garage. We have charging at the Car and Driver office, but I needed a proper setup at home to support all of the EVs we review.

I was able to add a 40-amp circuit to the existing electric service in my house without a pricy upgrade to run additional capacity, so that's why I landed on a 40-amp outlet versus a 50-amp setup.

To be able to switch easily among the units, I ordered the NEMA 14-50 plug-in variant of each charging device. (Note: Tesla doesn't sell a version of its Wall Connector with a plug, so to keep our test comparable, I wired one in myself to connect to my NEMA 14-50 outlet.)

In the first round of testing, I used each unit to charge our long-term Tesla Model 3 numerous times over a period of months. I then compared the electricity output from the wall to what the Model 3 reported made it into its battery pack using the third-party (and very cool) TeslaFi software.

Since then, I've tested many other units along with the favorites from before using our long-term Rivian R1T, BMW i4, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Kia EV9, and Lucid Air Pure, plus many other EVs and PHEVs we're reviewing. Despite varying cord lengths and thicknesses, there was no measurable difference in performance or efficiency (which averaged roughly 5 to 8 percent charging losses).

If you're an electric-vehicle owner who wants to start charging at home, here's what you need to know.

This is how much charging power is being sent to your EV, which is measured in kilowatts. (The voltage of the electrical circuit times the amps of current flowing equals the power in watts; 1000 watts equals a kilowatt. For example, a 240-volt outlet drawing 32 amps of current is outputting 7.7 kilowatts of power.)

A connector is what you need to connect your charging equipment to your EV. For at-home chargers like the products on this list, there are two main types to keep an eye out for: J1772 and Tesla's North American Charging Standard (NACS or J3400). Thankfully, adapters to switch between connector types are widely available, so limiting your purchase to whatever connection your vehicle features isn't necessary.

Cost really depends on if you have enough spare electrical capacity. If so, you might be able to run a new line for a few hundred dollars. If not, adding capacity to your home's electrical system can cost a few thousand. More on that below.

The sweeping Inflation Reduction Act reinstated a federal tax credit of 30 percent of your total costs (capped at $1000). Electrical upgrades, wiring, and the charger itself all qualify for this credit, but you'll want to act fast, as it's set to expire on June 30, 2026.

Your home's electrical circuit is rated for a certain amount of maximum amperage. Since EV charging can demand anywhere from 24 to 80 amps, it's important to see what additional capacity your home has above your current electrical needs, including furnace, air conditioning, oven, clothes dryer, etc.

Check the main fuse in your breaker box to see the amperage rating—that's the maximum your home can handle before blowing that main breaker. If you have 150- or 200-amp service or higher, you may have enough wiggle room to add charging without an upgrade. But you'll need to measure your house's peak electrical use and consult an electrician. We recommend using a modest 40- or 50-amp circuit due to its ability to charge most EVs overnight while keeping down install costs. Plus, when not charging a vehicle, you could use that 240-volt outlet for other items, such as an electric heater or welder. You will need a certified electrician to verify your home's circuit capacity and install any equipment or upgrades necessary.

Some EV-charging equipment, such as this Emporia unit, provides load management, which means it constantly monitors your house's overall output and will automatically lower the charging draw if necessary to prevent exceeding your house's capacity.

The charge rate is expressed in kilowatts of power—volts times amps equals watts, 1000 watts equals a kilowatt—which can be used to estimate charge time. If you're charging at 6 kilowatts and your EV has a 60.0-kWh battery, the charge time from empty to full will be roughly 10 hours. (It will actually be slightly longer due to losses during charging and the slowing of the charge rate as the battery nears 100 percent.) The charge rate is affected by three factors and will be limited to the lowest of these: the output of the household circuit, the charging equipment, and the vehicle's onboard charger.

If you wish to keep track of your EV's electrical use and cost, you'll want a home-charging unit with Wi-Fi connectivity. This allows you to monitor charging, receive alerts, and control the unit via an app.

Most of these EV chargers offer different variants to suit your needs. These variants (hard-wired or plug, different output capabilities, different connector types, and varying cord lengths) are typically offered at slightly different prices. Make sure you look at all the various options from any manufacturer.

If you'd like your EV charger to be mounted outside, it's perfectly doable. Each charging unit we tested has an outdoor-grade rating according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) or Ingress Protection (IP) standards. There's additional information on deciphering these ratings in our FAQs section below.

What are the different types of EV chargers?

Charging capability is categorized into three tiers. Level 1 and Level 2 use 120-volt and 240-volt AC electricity, respectively, which is what your house is wired for.

Level 3, also called DC fast-charging, is high-voltage (400 to 800 volts) DC charging that takes place at a dedicated public EV charger and charges far faster. DC fast-chargers can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to install, so it's not something you'd put in at home.

Home-charging equipment is analogous to a USB cable to charge your phone. It connects the electricity in your house to your car, and in that way they're all similar.

The main differences are their output capability—typically expressed in either amps (e.g., 32, 40, 48 amps) or power (e.g., 7.7, 9.6, 11.5 kW), which equates to charging speed—and whether they are Wi-Fi connected, which typically allows charging to be monitored and controlled remotely via a phone app.

The other main difference is whether the unit plugs in to an outlet or is hardwired into the circuit. Many providers sell units that come in either configuration, as well as with different plug types, while others, such as Tesla, are only offered in a hardwired configuration.

What's the difference between Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 charging?

The charging "Levels" generally refer to charging speed. Level 1 is extremely slow (think multiple days for a full charge), Level 2 is adequate for at-home use (an EV can charge overnight), and Level 3 is the fastest (a half-hour top-up might add 80 percent charge). Technically, the difference is the voltage at which energy is input into an EV.

Level 1 means 120 volts, like a typical household outlet, with a typical charging rate of about 1 kilowatt. Level 2 is 240 volts (like an electric dryer) and, depending on the amperage of the circuit, can range between about 6 and 19 kW. Level 3, DC fast-charging, typically operates at 400 or 800 volts, and the rates can be as high as 350 kW.

Not necessarily. While you do need a device to connect the electricity from your house to your vehicle, you may be able to get by with the portable charging equipment that came with your vehicle.

In some cases, the car either comes with or the automaker sells accessory adapters that allow the portable unit to plug into a 240-volt circuit and provide perfectly acceptable charging speeds, as long as you don't mind leaving it behind in your garage (or regularly loading it in and out of your car).

Which plug type should I choose for my charging equipment?

Although several automakers have announced a switch from a J1772 connector to Tesla's North America Charging Standard (NACS) design in the 2025–2026 time frame, whether you buy a J1772 or NACS unit today doesn't limit its future compatibility.

There are adapters to go from NACS to J1772 or vice versa, and with the mixed ports both on the vehicles and the public-charging infrastructure, EV owners will need to get used to keeping adapters in their vehicles to be prepared for whichever plug type they encounter.

Can charging equipment be mounted outside?

Generally, yes. Each charging unit we tested has an outdoor-grade rating according to either the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) or Ingress Protection (IP) standards. A NEMA 3R rating, like the ChargePoint and Tesla Wall Connector have, is intended for outdoor use, but does not mean watertight; under certain circumstances, moisture could potentially enter the enclosure.

The NEMA 4X rating of the Grizzl-E is superior. The IP ratings are two digits, the first representing the unit's resistance to solids (in this case dust) and the second number representing water protection. An IP66 rating means the unit is intended for outdoor use, with complete protection from dust or high-pressure water. But an IP67 goes one step further and can be immersed in water up to three feet deep.

Another thing to keep in mind with charging equipment mounted outside is that the electrical feed line to that location must also be in an outdoor-rated enclosure and, if you’re using a plug-type unit like we tested, that the outlet's enclosure must also be rated for outdoor use.

How do I wire my house to charge an EV and how much does it cost?

A good middle ground is a 40- or 50-amp circuit, which will be able to charge most EVs overnight. EV charging equipment can either connect via a plug or be hardwired into your home's electricity.

We suggest going with a NEMA 14-50 outlet; that way the charging equipment simply plugs into an outlet, similar to any other household device. If you move, you can unplug your pricey EV charging equipment and take it with you, or you can easily switch to another unit in the future. Plus, when you're not charging, that outlet could be used for other 240-volt needs, such as an electric heater or a welder.

In either case the EV charging hardware can only operate continuously at 80 percent of the capability of the circuit. So, a 50-amp circuit—i.e., the circuit has a 50-amp breaker—can charge at up to 40 amps (or 9.6 kW), or a 40-amp circuit at 32 amps (7.7 kW). The maximum current for a plug-type charging unit is a 50-amp circuit (40 amps continuous), while a hardwired circuit can go as high as 100 amps (80 amps continuous). That equates to a charging rate of 19.2 kW, which is the fastest possible with a Level 2 connection.

A dedicated electrical line must be run from your breaker box to the garage or exterior location where you want to install the charging equipment. Qmerit is a company that specializes in these installs and has a nationwide network of electrical contractors to do the work.

If your house has enough spare electrical capacity, you may be able to simply run a new line, which might cost a few hundred dollars. If not, more capacity needs to be added to your house, and that might raise the total to a couple of thousand dollars.

What's the difference between a vehicle's onboard charger and an EV charger?

Although many people refer to the products reviewed here as "chargers," technically they are electric-vehicle supply equipment, or EVSE. The vehicle's onboard charger is a device that converts the AC electricity from your house to DC energy to be stored in the battery, and it determines the fastest Level 2 charging rate your vehicle can handle. No matter how much electrical output you have at your house, you can't exceed the charge rate limited by the vehicle's onboard charger.

The Wallbox unit itself is lighter and smaller than most—it's roughly an eight-by-eight-inch square—so it doesn't take up much wall real estate. The app has a clean look, is easy to use, and has the usual features, such as the ability to schedule charge times based on variable electricity rates or any other preference. However, the pricing function lacks the ability to track a variable rate like the ChargePoint and Emporia will do. Like Emporia, Wallbox offers a load-sharing function, but it requires buying the company's very pricy $449 power meter.

Overall, we found the Wallbox to work well, but it doesn't offer any above-and-beyond features to justify a price that's higher than that of our top-rated models.

If you own a classic or other vehicle that spends a lot of time sitting, you're probably familiar with the Battery Tender brand, which sells a lot of trickle chargers for 12-volt batteries. The company more recently started offering a couple Level 2 options for charging EVs. We tested the 40-amp unit (9.6 kW max), which is the lower of the two wall-mounted options, and has one unique feature: The ability to require swiping a RFID card to start charging as a way to prevent unwanted users from accessing it. That could be a handy feature if your charging equipment is mounted outside but, unfortunately, disabling that setting can be done by anyone with access to the unit (no passcode or anything), which completely defeats the purpose.

While the Battery Tender is already one of the most expensive in the test, the higher-output 48-amp (11.5 kW) version costs even more. Unlike most of the competition, the Battery Tender doesn't offer Wi-Fi connectivity for control or energy monitoring. Instead, the energy consumed is displayed on a built-in 4.3-inch display while charging and briefly after unplugging. We'd generally prefer the ease of remote connectivity, but if your mounting location is out of range of your Wi-Fi, this is an option. Unfortunately, the readout is very simple, and there are no extra frills, such as scrolling back through past charges. The unit itself is one of the largest and bulkiest in our roundup, too.

I am an automotive engineer turned writer with more than 20 years of experience testing and reviewing cars. With the advent of the modern EV, I've thrown myself into learning everything I can about motors, batteries, and charging. This roundup of home EV-charging units isn't simply a distinct test that happened over days or weeks after which I moved on to something else. It's an ongoing way of life for me as I'm constantly driving and reviewing new EVs and continually evaluating the charging side of the equation while the vehicles are plugged in overnight, and I'm always looking for the best new units to evaluate.Car and Driver has been testing cars since 1956, and we continue to measure the maximum acceleration, braking, and cornering performance of many hundreds of vehicles every year. In addition, we measure everything from cargo capacity to how much a vehicle's pillars block outward visibility to real-world fuel economy at 75 mph. When you read one of our reviews, you're getting the value of decades of hands-on automotive experience and knowledge.

More recently, we've added new tests to measure the burgeoning class of electric vehicles. Those include a range test at a steady 75-mph highway speed and a fast-charging test from 10 percent to 90 percent state of charge. You can read more about our extensive vehicle testing here. We know and love cars and live and breathe them all day, every day.

The Gear Team helps readers make informed purchasing choices about automotive gear, tools, and accessories through hands-on product evaluations and comprehensive testing. Car and Driver's renowned testing standards mandate that we use all products we feature and that our findings and recommendations are based on personal experience and knowledge—not hype. We won't claim to have tested something we haven't, and we'll never recommend a product we wouldn't buy ourselves.

The Gear Team's product selection and gear picks are editorially independent; Car and Driver has a strict policy against accepting payment for placement in articles.

We've evaluated dozens of product categories, including floor mats, tire inflators, and car covers. Visit our Tested & Trusted collection to see the very best in automotive gear. Read more about our testing process here.

Dave VanderWerp has spent more than 20 years in the automotive industry, in varied roles from engineering to product consulting, and now leading Car and Driver's vehicle-testing efforts. #4348. Gen.G recover from opening loss to beat LYON 2-1 and reach Worlds 2026 quarter-finals

Gen.G completed a 3-0 Swiss Stage run at Worlds 2026 on Sunday by coming from a game down to beat LYON 2-1. The LCK champions are through to the quarter-finals, while LYON must look to Round 4 to join them.

The best-of-three series began at 20:55 on Sunday 25 October 2026.

Earlier in the evening, on the third day of the Swiss Stage, Dplus KIA swept Movistar KOI 2-0. Smash scored the first pentakill of the tournament in game one of that series.

The Swiss Stage runs over five rounds. Teams reaching three match wins advance to the Knockout Stage. Teams reaching three defeats are eliminated. Gen.G’s run began with 1-0 wins over Invictus Gaming and Hanwha Life Esports.

LYON controlled game one. They took Baron as soon as it spawned at 20 minutes without losing a player. A second Baron followed after a five-versus-five fight, and LYON pushed on to the Nexus. Dot Esports picked out jungler Inspired and bot laner Berserker, on Kalista, as LYON’s key performers. On the other side, Canyon’s Qiyana kept missing his ultimates.

Gen.G responded quickly. A convincing top-lane teamfight at 23 minutes gave them Baron and the Dragon Soul, and the series was level. In the decider, Gen.G lost Galio early in a teamfight. Kiin then joined on Camille via Teleport. Gen.G went on to break the mid inhibitor, collect three dragons and win the final fight.

On paper, the gap between the sides was wide. Gen.G sit fourth in the Elo power rankings with a rating of 1868 and a 118-30 record. LYON are 28th with a rating of 1720 and a 34-28 record.

The defeat was LYON’s first at the event. They had opened with 1-0 wins over Team Secret Whales and Karmine Corp. They go into Round 4 with a 2-1 record. One more match win would send them to the Knockout Stage.

#4346. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

#4345. ‘Billie’ Is a 650-HP Modified Pontiac GTO from Ringbrothers

Ringbrothers is back at SEMA with a customized 1965 Pontiac, featuring carbon-fiber bodywork and an LT4 supercharged V-8 engine.

The 2026 SEMA show opened today, celebrating the unbridled imagination of the custom car scene, and, of course, Wisconsin-based Ringbrothers has returned with yet another exquisite creation. This year’s showpiece is a 1965 Pontiac GTO convertible dubbed “Billie,” which enhances the classic muscle car’s assertive styling and packs it with modern power.

Ringbrothers built Billie for a customer who wanted to pay tribute to a GTO his mother once owned. The client originally proposed the name “Goat,” with Ringbrothers suggesting Billie (as in billy goat), a more playful take on the iconic Pontiac’s long-held nickname.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147

Despite presenting as a GTO, Billie originally started life as a 1965 Pontiac Tempest, before Ringbrothers went to work, widening the body by five inches, reshaping the front fenders, lengthening the rocker panels, and adding carbon-fiber doors. The hood is also fashioned from carbon fiber and wears billet-aluminum inserts and an enlarged scoop to feed air to the engine.

That engine is a Chevy’s LT4 supercharged 6.2-liter V-8, cranking out 650 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque and hooked up to a Bowler Performance 10-speed automatic transmission. The body is placed atop a Roadster Shop Fast Track Stage III chassis, and Billie also features Fox coil-over springs and six-piston Brembo brakes. The staggered HRE G-Code wheels, measuring 19 inches up front and 20 inches at the rear, are shod in Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 rubber.

At first glance, Billie looks quite faithful to the original GTO, but look closely, and you’ll notice custom bumpers, new headlight surrounds, and a single-piece machined billet-aluminum taillight panel. Ringbrothers also employed carbon fiber on the lower front end and for the rear bumper section that houses the large exhaust outlets. Adding to the head-turning look is the Billie Goat Blue paint job, a rich, shimmering hue that is contrasted by polished chrome trim.

The cabin is outfitted in gray and blue leather, while the dashboard has been pushed four inches forward and two inches lower. Ringbrothers modernized the instrumentation, fitted a new climate-control system, and added an auto-dimming rearview mirror. There’s also a restored factory radio that now has Bluetooth connectivity, and the aluminum trim is paired with a sweet wood shifter.

Ringbrothers says the entire build took more than 5500 hours. Billie may not be as radical as some of Ringbrothers’ past projects, such as the LT4-powered Rolls-Royce dubbed “Paramount” or “Enyo,” a 1948 Chevy truck turned into an open-wheel race car, but the modified Pontiac is the perfect representation of the company’s expertise in honing the classic lines of vintage muscle cars.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.
